title: Fine-tuning lab: LLMs on ConvFinQA
text:
Preface
This book is a hands-on lab for learning LLM fine-tuning with Hugging Face, using the ConvFinQA conversational question-answering task (Chen et al. 2022). It explains how models work, runs the experiments, and records the results.
The full roadmap lives in PLAN.md in the repository root.






Chen, Zhiyu, Shiyang Li, Charese Smiley, Zhiqiang Ma, Sameena Shah, and William Yang Wang. 2022. “ConvFinQA: Exploring the Chain of Numerical Reasoning in Conversational Finance Question Answering.” Proceedings of EMNLP.

title: 1  Environment setup
text:
1.1 Python environment and Quarto
This lab uses uv for Python environment setup. Run uv sync from the project root to create the virtual environment in .venv.
In VS Code, the repository’s .vscode/settings.json selects .venv as the Python interpreter, and the Quarto extension passes it to Quarto (our document generator). If a render fails with No module named 'yaml' or “Jupyter is not available”, start a new terminal (or reload the window) so that it picks up the project interpreter.

title: 1  Environment setup
section: 1.2 How to render this Quarto book
text:
1.2 How to render this Quarto book
Run these from the project root:
quarto preview docs/ --no-execute-daemon   # live preview while you write; re-renders a chapter when you save it
quarto render docs/      # render the whole book (the recommended way to build it)
What is re-executed. Every chapter uses Quarto’s freeze: auto. A chapter is re-executed, in full, only when its own .qmd file changes, and otherwise its saved results in docs/_freeze/ are reused. Quarto does not notice changes to the Python package in src/convfinqa/, to docs/_environment, or to the data. To force a re-run of one chapter, delete its folder docs/_freeze/<chapter>/, or run quarto render docs/<chapter>.qmd --no-execute-daemon.
Heavy cells. Some computations, such as training and full evaluation, take minutes to hours. Results are stored as named artifacts in artifacts/, each with a node.json that records its configuration and the artifacts it was built from. On later renders a chapter loads the saved result instead of recomputing, so editing a chapter’s text stays cheap. If an upstream artifact changes, everything built from it counts as stale.
Cells marked #HEAVY will not recompute a stale or missing artifact on their own: they raise an error that names the build command. The error is deliberate, because a preview or an ordinary render can never start a long run by accident. Setting ALLOW_STALE=1 relaxes this for artifacts that exist but are out of date: the cell loads the old result and shows a red warning box above it. A missing artifact always raises.
Declaring an artifact. The recipe sits in the chapter, in the cell that uses the result: a function decorated with @artifact(...), followed by the call that loads it. Artifact names use letters, digits and underscores, and a name template such as sft_{variant}_{seed} covers a family (get("sft_dsl_0") is one member). The function is only a few lines of glue that call the real logic in src/convfinqa/, and it may use only its own parameters, builtins and imports made inside it, so that a build in a separate process finds everything it needs. The function must be a plain def at the top level of its cell (not inside an if or a function), and a cell marked #| eval: false is ignored, so use a plain python fence to show an example. Quarto never has to run a chapter for the build script to know its artifacts: the registry reads the .qmd files and finds the recipes and the get("name") calls by parsing them (a get may appear anywhere in a cell, inside flow control too).
What makes an artifact stale. An artifact is rebuilt when any of these changed: its parameters or declared input files; the source of its builder function, or of any convfinqa module the function imports (whitespace, comments and docstrings don’t count, and neither do other cells or the chapter’s prose); its builder’s manual version; or any artifact it was built from, which in turn must itself be fresh. A rebuild that produces identical output leaves everything downstream fresh. Every build seeds Python, NumPy and torch from the artifact’s seed first, so its random draws do not depend on what ran before it. GPU training is still not bit-reproducible, so retraining normally yields new weights and the evaluations built on them are rebuilt too.
Building everything. Before each render, a hook (pre-render in docs/_quarto.yml) marks the chapters that used a changed artifact for re-execution, so nothing stale is left in the book. A heavy build can take hours, so it has to survive a lost terminal. The way to build the book is the script build.sh in the project root:
./build.sh
It does four things:

Inside a screen session named render, builds every missing or stale artifact in dependency order (python -m convfinqa.artifacts build --all), each heavy one in its own process that logs to artifacts/<name>/build.log; then runs quarto render docs/ --no-execute-daemon --log artifacts/render.log without RUN_HEAVY, so anything still stale fails loudly instead of starting a hidden run. The session keeps running if your terminal or connection drops. Detach with Ctrl-a d and reattach later with screen -r render.
Waits for the session to finish, whether or not you stay attached. It writes its exit status to artifacts/render.status, and the script polls for it.
Starts quarto preview docs/ only if that succeeded, with ALLOW_STALE=1, so editing prose keeps working after a code change made an artifact stale (the warning box marks the old result). The preview never starts a build. A failure prints its exit code instead, and a killed session is reported rather than waited on forever.
Refuses to start if a render session already exists (“Render already in progress”), so two builds cannot run at once through the script.

That last guard covers only builds started through build.sh. It looks for the screen session by name. A build started some other way, such as uv run python -m convfinqa.artifacts build --all typed directly, or a tmux session, is invisible to it. A per-artifact lock stops two processes building the same artifact, but two renders writing to docs/_book/ at once can corrupt each other, so start every full build through build.sh. (RUN_HEAVY=1 quarto render docs/ also still works, building stale heavy artifacts as the chapters reach them, in chapter order rather than dependency order.)
Why --no-execute-daemon. By default Quarto keeps a chapter’s Jupyter kernel alive for five minutes after rendering it, and the next render of that chapter reuses it. A reused kernel keeps the environment variables it started with, so a later RUN_HEAVY=1 or ALLOW_STALE=1 would be silently ignored, and it keeps whatever code it already loaded. The flag gives every render a fresh kernel. (Setting execute: daemon: false in _quarto.yml looked like the same thing but had no effect in Quarto 1.10.19, which we checked.) The artifact registry also re-reads the chapter files when they change, so an edited builder is never served stale even inside a long-lived kernel.
Quarto’s --log option is used instead of piping through tee, because Quarto writes terminal colour codes to a pipe and the log file stays free of them. Each render overwrites artifacts/render.log, so copy it if you want to keep one. The per-artifact build logs in artifacts/<name>/build.log are separate (a failed build leaves its log in artifacts/<name>.tmp/). If a build fails, nothing renders; fix the problem and run ./build.sh again, and the artifacts that were already built are reused.
To see what a full render would build, or to build one artifact without Quarto:
uv run python -m convfinqa.artifacts status           # what is fresh, stale or missing, and why
uv run python -m convfinqa.artifacts build sft_dsl_0  # build one artifact and anything stale it needs
uv run python -m convfinqa.artifacts refresh           # re-execute chapters that used outdated artifacts (the pre-render hook does this)

title: 1  Environment setup
section: 1.3 The hardware and the CUDA stack
text:
1.3 The hardware and the CUDA stack
Three different tools report a “CUDA version”, and they mean different things.

nvidia-smi reports the newest CUDA runtime the driver supports.
torch.version.cuda is the CUDA runtime bundled in the PyTorch wheel.
nvcc --version is the compiler installed on the system, used only if we compile CUDA extensions.

Drivers are compatible across minor versions, so these need not match. Here they agree, as the output below shows.


Code
import subprocess
import torch

smi = subprocess.run(
    ["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=name,driver_version", "--format=csv,noheader"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
).stdout.strip()

nvcc = subprocess.run(
    ["nvcc", "--version"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
).stdout.strip().splitlines()[-2]

smi_cuda = [
    l for l in subprocess.run(
        ["nvidia-smi"], capture_output=True, text=True
    ).stdout.splitlines()
    if "CUDA Version" in l
][0].split("CUDA Version:")[1].split()[0]

print("GPU / driver :", smi)
print("nvidia-smi   : CUDA", smi_cuda)
print("torch.cuda   :", torch.version.cuda)
print("nvcc         :", nvcc.strip())

import re

nvcc_cuda = re.search(r"release (\d+\.\d+)", " ".join(
    subprocess.run(["nvcc", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True)
    .stdout.splitlines()
)).group(1)
assert smi_cuda == torch.version.cuda == nvcc_cuda  # the sentence below


GPU / driver : NVIDIA GB10, 595.99.02
nvidia-smi   : CUDA 13.2
torch.cuda   : 13.2
nvcc         : Cuda compilation tools, release 13.2, V13.2.86


All three say CUDA 13.2.

1.4 Does bf16 work?
This lab uses bf16 for the model computations on the GB10 GPU. This uses 8 exponent bits as in standard 32-bit floating point (fp32), but only 7 mantissa bits, reducing precision. In return, bf16 allows for faster computation and reduced memory usage on compatible hardware.

Computational expressions generated by the model for generating the final outputs will use exact arithmetic; only the model’s own computation runs in reduced precision.

assert c.dtype == torch.bfloat16 and torch.isfinite(c.float()).all()

title: 2  What ConvFinQA looks like
text:
2.1 Getting the data
You will learn:
ConvFinQA (Chen et al. 2022) turns FinQA questions about earnings-report pages into multi-turn conversations. Each page has text before a table, the table, and text after it. A conversation asks a chain of questions about that page, and each turn has a small program in a domain-specific language (DSL) that computes the answer.
The code lives in src/convfinqa/data/. The download clones the authors’ repository and unzips data.zip into data/raw/, and does nothing if the data is already there.
Code
import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.dsl import steps

data.download_data()

splits = {
    name: data.load_split(name)
    for name in ["train", "dev", "test", "train_turn", "dev_turn"]
}

pd.DataFrame({
    "rows": {k: len(v) for k, v in splits.items()},
    "has labels": {
        k: "annotation" in v[0] and "turn_program" in v[0]["annotation"]
        for k, v in splits.items()
    }
})

2.2 One record
A conversation is a JSON object. The fields we use are pre_text, table, post_text, and under annotation: dialogue_break (the questions), turn_program, exe_ans_list (the answers) and qa_split (see Type II below).

title: 2  What ConvFinQA looks like
text:
2.3 A Type I conversation
Type I conversations decompose one FinQA question into a chain of turns. First the page the model sees: the text before the table (shortened here), the table as markdown, and the text after.


Code
from IPython.display import Markdown

def show_page(conv, n=300):
    pre = " ".join(conv["pre_text"])
    post = " ".join(conv["post_text"])
    return Markdown(
        f"*pre_text ({len(conv['pre_text'])} sentences):* …{pre[-n:]}\n\n"
        + data.table_to_markdown(conv["table"])
        + f"\n\n*post_text ({len(conv['post_text'])} sentences):* {post[:n]}…"
    )

show_page(conv_I)

Then the conversation, one turn per line: question, gold program, and the number the program computes.

print(data.format_conversation(conv_I))


Single_AAPL/2002/page_23.pdf-1  (Type I)
  [1] Q: what was the total of net sales in 2001?
      program: 5363
      answer:  5363
  [2] Q: and what was that in 2000?
      program: 7983
      answer:  7983
  [3] Q: what was, then, the change in the total of net sales over the year?
      program: subtract(5363, 7983)
      answer:  -2620
  [4] Q: and how much does this change represent in relation to that total in 2000, in percentage?
      program: subtract(5363, 7983), divide(#0, 7983)
      answer:  -0.3282


The first turns just select a number from the table. Later turns compute with them. The last turn restates the full calculation, using #0 for “the result of step 0” so the program stays self-contained.

The raw table_ori shows what went wrong. The header was split across two rows:

for row in conv_garbled["table_ori"][:3]:
    print(row)


['', 'Year ended June 30, 2009']
['2008', '2007']
['Net income', '$103,102', '$104,222', '$104,681']


Read together, the first two rows are a single header row, ['', 'Year ended June 30, 2009', '2008', '2007'], whose first label was extracted on a separate line from the other two. The cleaned table then built a header from the broken pieces: its columns repeat fragments of “year ended june 30 2009”, and the year labels also show up in pre_text (the trailing : 2009 2008 2007 .). This is how the data ships, not a parsing error of ours.
The model must work out that the columns are 2009, 2008 and 2007 from the table and the surrounding text, which is part of the task.

Type II conversations merge two FinQA questions about the same page. qa_split marks which turns belong to which: 0s, then 1s.

title: 2  What ConvFinQA looks like
text:
2.6 The DSL
A program is a comma-separated list of steps, op(arg, arg). A turn that only selects a number has a bare number as its program. The operations are add, subtract, multiply, divide, exp and greater. (The authors’ code also lists FinQA’s table_sum, table_average, table_max and table_min, but no ConvFinQA gold program uses them.) An argument is one of:

a number literal copied from the page, such as 206588 or 0.14136, possibly with a % sign, such as 19%;
a step reference #k, the result of step k;
a constant from a fixed list.

The chapter on the DSL and its executor covers the grammar and the executor in detail. Here we look at what makes an argument a literal or a constant, and how the paper’s model decides what it may write.

2.6.1 Constants
The constants are not read from the page. The authors’ code defines a fixed list of constants, and every constant in the train and dev programs is in it:


Code
import re

const_use = Counter(
    c
    for s in ["train", "dev"]
    for conv in splits[s]
    for p in conv["annotation"]["turn_program"]
    for c in re.findall(r"const_\w+", p)
)
assert set(const_use) <= set(steps.CONSTANTS)

pd.Series(
    {c: const_use.get(c, 0) for c in steps.CONSTANTS},
    name="uses (train + dev)"
).to_frame().T

The list has 18 constants.
They are mostly scale factors and counts: const_100 turns a ratio into a percentage, const_1000 and const_1000000 convert units, and small integers such as const_3 count years for an average (the Type II example above ends with divide(#1, const_3)). The rule is by convention, not by whether the digits occur on the page: a number the question needs but does not read from the document is a constant, and the same digits read off the page are a literal.


2.6.2 Percentages and the executor
The official executor (str_to_num in the authors’ general_utils.py) strips commas and tries to read a float. If that fails and the string contains %, it removes the sign and divides by 100, so 19% is evaluated as 0.19. A const_ token is replaced by its number (const_m1 is -1). The executor never looks at the page: whether a program may use 19% at all is decided elsewhere.


2.6.3 What the paper’s decoder may write
FinQANet’s generator (Chen et al. 2022) is restricted: at each step it can emit an operator, a constant from the list, a step reference, or a number copied from its input. Its input is the question plus the context it is given (supporting text and table rows), split on spaces, and a token counts as a copyable number if, after removing commas, it parses as a number or ends with %. This is the rule, implemented in steps.copyable_numbers:


Code
row = " ".join(conv_I["table"][-1])
print(row)
print(steps.copyable_numbers(row))


gross margin percentage 28% ( 28 % ) 23% ( 23 % ) 27% ( 27 % )
['28%', '28', '%', '23%', '23', '%', '27%', '27', '%']


This works because the page text is pre-tokenized: punctuation and symbols are separated from the surrounding text by spaces ($ 103102, june 30 , 2009, ( 2913 )), so numbers can be extracted cleanly. The exception is %, which the data keeps attached to its number in the first form (28%) and also writes as a separate token in the parenthesised form (( 28 % )). The attached 28% is a candidate. In the spaced form, 28 is a candidate and the lone % also passes the rule, which looks like an accidental quirk of the check.
Whether our own models should be restricted this way is a separate question, taken up in the constrained-decoding chapter.

title: 2  What ConvFinQA looks like
text:
2.7 How big is it?


Code
rows = []
for split in ["train", "dev"]:
    for c in splits[split]:
        for t in data.turns(c):
            rows.append({
                "split": split,
                "id": c["id"],
                "type": data.conversation_type(c),
                "turn": t.index + 1,
                "number_turn": steps.is_number_turn(t.program),
                "program": t.program
            })
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

per_conv = df.groupby(["split", "id", "type"]).size()\
    .rename("turns").reset_index()

summary = per_conv.groupby("split").agg(
    conversations=("id", "count"),
    turns=("turns", "sum"),
    mean_turns=("turns", "mean")
)

summary["type II share"] = per_conv.assign(ii=per_conv.type == "II")\
    .groupby("split").ii.mean()

Turns per conversation (train + dev) and the share of number-selection vs. program turns.




The DSL operations are counted from the new step each turn adds: the last step of its program, since each program repeats the earlier steps.


Code
ops = Counter()
for p in df[(df.split == "train") & ~df.number_turn].program:
    ops[steps.split_steps(p)[-1].split("(")[0]] += 1

title: 2  What ConvFinQA looks like
section: 2.8 How long is a conversation in tokens?
text:
2.8 How long is a conversation in tokens?
Training uses one sequence per full conversation: the system prompt, the page, and every question and answer. So the longest conversations set the memory we need. Turning a data row into token ids takes three steps:

Row to messages. Our own choice, in conversation_messages (src/convfinqa/formatting.py): a system prompt, then the page and the first question as the first user message, then the gold program as the assistant’s reply, and so on for every turn. The experiments part extends this module for training.
Messages to one string. The model’s own chat template, which ships with its tokenizer. It wraps each message in the special markers that the model was trained with.
String to token ids. The tokenizer itself.

Here is step 2 for the clean Type I conversation from above. The page text and table are cut out so the structure is visible.


Code
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")

text = tok.apply_chat_template(conversation_messages(conv_I), tokenize=False)
cut = text.index("\n\nQuestion:")
print(text[:260] + "\n[... page text and table omitted ...]" + text[cut:])

Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL.<|im_end|>

[... page text and table omitted ...]

The <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> markers delimit each message and carry its role. The model learns to end every answer with <|im_end|>, and that token is part of what we train on.






NoteWhich tokenizer, and why it matters



The ConvFinQA paper doesn’t prescribe a tokenizer; it predates our model. We use the tokenizer and chat template of the model we will fine-tune, Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, so that the lengths below are what training will see. The numbers, and the max_length we derive from them, belong to this tokenizer and to our formatting. A different base model would give slightly different counts, so check them again before reusing the value.


Now we count tokens for every conversation of train and dev (step 3). The count is made by convfinqa.lengths, with add_special_tokens=False because the template has already written the special tokens into the string. It is the artifact conversation_lengths, so that the chapters that need the longest conversation read it from there, and a rebuild from a clean checkout makes it again.


Code
import pandas as pd

from convfinqa.artifacts import artifact, get


@artifact("conversation_lengths")
def build_conversation_lengths(out, deps):
    import json

    from transformers import AutoTokenizer

    from convfinqa import data
    from convfinqa.lengths import conversation_lengths, max_length_for

    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")
    rows = conversation_lengths(
        tok, {name: data.load_split(name) for name in ["train", "dev"]}
    )
    longest = max(r["tokens"] for r in rows)
    (out / "lengths.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in rows)
    )
    (out / "lengths.json").write_text(json.dumps(
        {"longest": longest, "max_length": max_length_for(longest)}
    ))

NoteUnder the hood



Notice how numbers like 206588 cost one token per digit in this tokenizer. The foundations part looks at tokenization properly. It is one reason the model writes a program and a Python executor does the arithmetic.








TipFurther reading

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
text:
3.1 The grammar
You will learn:
The model never does arithmetic itself. It writes a program, and the executor computes the number. That makes each answer checkable, and it keeps exact arithmetic out of a model that reads numbers one digit at a time.
A program with no parentheses is a number-selection turn: its value is just that number. Every other program is a list of steps. Step k may refer to the result of any earlier step as #j with j < k. The last step’s result is the answer.
crumbs: 3  The DSL and its executor

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
text:
program   = number | step { "," step }
step      = operation "(" argument "," argument ")"
operation = "add" | "subtract" | "multiply" | "divide" | "exp" | "greater"
argument  = number | percent | "#" index | constant
number    = digits, optionally with commas and a decimal point, e.g. 206588 or 1,234.5
percent   = number "%"            # evaluated as number / 100
index     = digit { digit }       # the result of an earlier step
constant  = "const_" ( digits | "m1" )   # a fixed list of 18, see the chapter on what ConvFinQA looks like
crumbs: 3  The DSL and its executor

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
text:
3.2 Running a program


Code
import pandas as pd

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.dsl import executor

program = "subtract(206588, 181001), divide(#0, 181001)"
steps = executor.parse_program(program)
results = executor.trace(program)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "step": [f"#{i}" for i in range(len(steps))],
        "operation": [s.op for s in steps],
        "arguments": [", ".join(s.args) for s in steps],
        "result": [
            r if isinstance(r, str)
            else f"{round(r, executor.ROUND_DIGITS):g}" for r in results
        ],
    }
)

3.3 Conventions inherited from the official code
The executor follows eval_program and str_to_num in the authors’ code/utils/general_utils.py.

    "constant": "divide(300, const_3)",
    "negative constant": "multiply(5, const_m1)",
    "rounded to 5 places": "divide(2, 3)",
    "a tiny result rounds to 0": "divide(1, const_1000000)",

% divides by 100, so 0.25% is 0.0025.
Every result is rounded to 5 decimal places, which is also how the gold answers are stored.

Two answers match only when they are exactly equal after rounding: the official script has no numerical tolerance beyond that rounding.

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
text:
3.4 When a program is wrong
A model’s output can fail in several ways. The executor reports the kind of failure instead of raising an anonymous error, so the evaluation can count them separately.


Code
bad = {
    "empty output": "",
    "unbalanced parenthesis": "add(1, 2",
    "one argument": "add(1)",
    "nested call": "add(1, add(2, 3))",
    "unknown operator": "sqrt(4, 2)",
    "not a number": "add(one, 2)",
    "reference to a later step": "add(1, 2), add(#1, 2)",
    "division by zero": "divide(1, 0)",
    "complex result": "exp(-8, 0.5)",
}
rows = []
for label, p in bad.items():
    value, kind = executor.try_execute(p)
    rows.append({"failure": label, "program": p, "error kind": kind})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
section: 3.5 Do the gold programs reproduce the gold answers?
text:
3.5 Do the gold programs reproduce the gold answers?
The strongest test of the executor is the data: every turn’s turn_program must execute to its exe_ans_list entry.


Code
rows = []
for split in ["train", "dev"]:
    n = mismatches = 0
    for conv in data.load_split(split):
        a = conv["annotation"]
        for prog, gold in zip(a["turn_program"], a["exe_ans_list"]):
            n += 1
            if not executor.answers_match(executor.try_execute(prog)[0], gold):
                mismatches += 1
    rows.append({
        "split": split,
        "turns": n,
        "mismatches": mismatches,
        "match rate": 1 - mismatches / n
    })
result = pd.DataFrame(rows)
assert (result.mismatches == 0).all()
result

title: 3  The DSL and its executor
section: 3.6 Where our executor differs from the official one
text:
3.6 Where our executor differs from the official one

table_* operations are rejected as unknown operators. The authors’ code supports table_sum, table_average, table_max and table_min, but no ConvFinQA gold program uses them.
Errors are reported by kind. The official function returns a single invalid flag.
Syntax is checked with a fixed pattern. The official code checks structure by token position. Ours parses each step as operation(argument, argument) and rejects, for example, nested calls and missing commas. All gold programs pass, so this does not change a gold score. We have not compared the two parsers on malformed model output.
#k must refer to an earlier step. A reference to itself or a later step is invalid. The official code reaches the same result through a lookup error.







NoteUnder the hood



The executor never looks at the page, so it cannot tell whether a number in a program was copied from the text or invented. The paper’s own model could only copy numbers from its input. Our fine-tuned model writes freely, and only the constrained-decoding chapter tests whether restricting it helps.








TipFurther reading



The official execution and evaluation code is code/utils/general_utils.py in the ConvFinQA repository (https://github.com/czyssrs/ConvFinQA). The paper (Chen et al. 2022) defines the operations and the metrics.








Chen, Zhiyu, Shiyang Li, Charese Smiley, Zhiqiang Ma, Sameena Shah, and William Yang Wang. 2022. “ConvFinQA: Exploring the Chain of Numerical Reasoning in Conversational Finance Question Answering.” Proceedings of EMNLP.

title: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities
text:
4.1 From text to tokens
You will learn:
A language model never sees letters or digits. It sees a sequence of integers. The tokenizer splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary and replaces each piece by its position in that vocabulary. This chapter works with the model we fine-tune later, Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.
Code
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.book.viz import show_tokens, tokenize

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")
print(f"vocabulary size: {len(tok):,}")


vocabulary size: 151,669
The helper show_tokens colours each token. Hover over a token to see its id. Examples come from the train split.
crumbs: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities

title: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities
text:
4.1.1 A question


Code
conv = {c["id"]: c for c in data.load_split("train")}[
    "Single_AAPL/2002/page_23.pdf-1"
]
question = conv["annotation"]["dialogue_break"][0]
show_tokens(tok, question)


what was the total of net sales in 2001?14 tokens, 40 characters


Common words are single tokens, and the space in front of a word belongs to the word: ␣was, ␣the. The year 2001 is not one token. It is four.


4.1.2 A table row


Code
row = data.table_to_markdown(conv["table"]).splitlines()[2]
show_tokens(tok, row)


| net sales | $ 5742 | $ 5363 | $ 7983 |25 tokens, 40 characters


The symbols and separators |, $ and the spaces around them cost tokens too. A table of a few dozen cells is already hundreds of tokens, which is why a whole report page makes a long prompt.


4.1.3 Numbers


Code
for text in ["206588", "0.14136", "1,234.5", "28%", "$ 5742"]:
    display(show_tokens(tok, text))


2065886 tokens, 6 characters


0.141367 tokens, 7 characters


1,234.57 tokens, 7 characters


28%3 tokens, 3 characters


$ 57426 tokens, 6 characters


Every digit is its own token. The same digits give the same tokens wherever they appear:


Code
display(show_tokens(
    tok,
    "net cash from operating activities was 181001 in 2008, so 181001 is the base"
))


net cash from operating activities was 181001 in 2008, so 181001 is the base31 tokens, 76 characters


The model never sees 181001 as one unit, only the digit sequence 1 8 1 0 0 1. This follows from the tokenizer’s design (see below), and it is one reason why we do not ask the model to do arithmetic itself. It writes a program, and the executor from Chapter 3 computes the number.


4.1.4 A gold program


Code
show_tokens(tok, conv["annotation"]["turn_program"][-1])


subtract(5363, 7983), divide(#0, 7983)23 tokens, 38 characters


The DSL was not designed for this tokenizer. Some pieces merge in surprising ways, such as ), and (#, and an operator takes its leading space with it (␣divide). Fine-tuning teaches the model to produce exactly this token sequence.


4.1.5 Another tokenizer, for contrast
GPT-2’s tokenizer has no rule that isolates digits. Its vocabulary merges digits that were frequent together in its training text, so the same number can be cut differently in different places.


Code
gpt2 = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
for text in ["206588", " 181001", "0.14136"]:
    print(f"GPT-2: {text!r}")
    display(show_tokens(gpt2, text))
    print(f"Qwen3: {text!r}")
    display(show_tokens(tok, text))


GPT-2: '206588'


2065883 tokens, 6 characters


Qwen3: '206588'


2065886 tokens, 6 characters


GPT-2: ' 181001'


 1810012 tokens, 7 characters


Qwen3: ' 181001'


 1810017 tokens, 7 characters


GPT-2: '0.14136'


0.141364 tokens, 7 characters


Qwen3: '0.14136'


0.141367 tokens, 7 characters


For arithmetic this is awkward either way, but Qwen’s digit-by-digit split is at least consistent: a digit is always one token, whatever its neighbours are.






NoteUnder the hood



Qwen’s tokenizer is a byte-level BPE tokenizer. Its vocabulary was built by starting from single bytes and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pairs in a large text corpus. Before any merging applies, a pre-tokenizer first splits the text with a regular expression. Part of Qwen’s expression is \p{N}, which matches a single digit, so a digit can never merge with its neighbours.


Code
import json

pre = json.loads(tok.backend_tokenizer.to_str())\
    ["pre_tokenizer"]["pretokenizers"][0]["pattern"]["Regex"]
print(pre)


(?i:'s|'t|'re|'ve|'m|'ll|'d)|[^\r\n\p{L}\p{N}]?\p{L}+|\p{N}| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+[\r\n]*|\s*[\r\n]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+

title: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities
text:
4.2 Tracing one prediction
Now we follow a single prediction through the model. The model’s only job is to read a sequence of tokens and say how likely each possible next token is. We take the first turn of the conversation from above, formatted as a chat, and stop right where the assistant’s answer begins.


Code
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages

# the system prompt and the first user turn
messages = conversation_messages(conv)[:2]

prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True
)

print("...", repr(prompt[-70:]))
gold = conv["annotation"]["turn_program"][0]
print("gold answer:", gold)


... 't was the total of net sales in 2001?<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n'
gold answer: 5363


The prompt ends with <|im_start|>assistant and a newline: the model is about to write its answer. The gold answer is 5363, so the right first token is 5. We load the model in bf16 on the GPU (the first run downloads about 8 GB).


Code
name = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, dtype=torch.bfloat16)\
    .to("cuda").eval()
cfg = model.config
print(f"{cfg.num_hidden_layers} layers, hidden size {cfg.hidden_size}, vocabulary rows {cfg.vocab_size:,}")


36 layers, hidden size 2560, vocabulary rows 151,936



4.2.1 Token ids


Code
ids = tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False, return_tensors="pt")\
    ["input_ids"].to("cuda")
print("shape:", tuple(ids.shape), "(batch, tokens)")
print(
    "last five ids:",
    ids[0, -5:].tolist(),
    [tok.decode([i]) for i in ids[0, -5:]]
)


shape: (1, 1125) (batch, tokens)
last five ids: [151645, 198, 151644, 77091, 198] ['<|im_end|>', '\n', '<|im_start|>', 'assistant', '\n']




4.2.2 Embeddings
Each id selects one row of a big table, the embedding matrix, which has one row per vocabulary entry. The row is a vector of 2,560 numbers that the model learned for that token.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    emb = model.model.embed_tokens(ids)
print("embedding matrix:", tuple(model.model.embed_tokens.weight.shape))
print("after lookup:", tuple(emb.shape), emb.dtype, "(batch, tokens, hidden)")


embedding matrix: (151936, 2560)
after lookup: (1, 1125, 2560) torch.bfloat16 (batch, tokens, hidden)




4.2.3 The transformer
The vectors pass through 36 transformer layers. Each layer adds an update to every position’s vector, so the vector is a running sum that every layer nudges, and its shape never changes. What happens inside a layer, attention across positions and a small network at each position, is the subject of the next chapter. For now the stack is a black box that maps vectors to vectors. We feed the embeddings from the previous step straight in. output_hidden_states keeps the vectors at every stage: entry 0 is the embeddings we put in, entry k is what layer k produced, and the last entry is the transformer’s final output, which is what the next step uses.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model.model(inputs_embeds=emb, output_hidden_states=True)
hidden = out.last_hidden_state
print("hidden states kept:", len(out.hidden_states), "= embeddings + 36 layers")
print("final hidden state:", tuple(hidden.shape))

# the last entry is the final output, and feeding ids instead
# gives the same result: the model simply does the embedding lookup itself
assert torch.equal(out.hidden_states[-1], hidden)
with torch.no_grad():
    assert torch.equal(hidden, model.model(input_ids=ids).last_hidden_state)


hidden states kept: 37 = embeddings + 36 layers
final hidden state: (1, 1125, 2560)


The meaning of a position’s vector changes on the way through. It starts as the embedding of token i. By the end it encodes a prediction for the token at position i + 1.


4.2.4 Logits
The last step turns each position’s vector into one score per vocabulary entry. These scores are the logits. A matrix with 151,936 rows, one per vocabulary entry, the language-model head, does the multiplication.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model.lm_head(hidden)
print("logits:", tuple(logits.shape), "(batch, tokens, vocabulary rows)")


logits: (1, 1125, 151936) (batch, tokens, vocabulary rows)


In this model the head’s weights are the embedding matrix itself (more on that at the end). So the score of a token is the dot product of the final vector with that token’s embedding: the final vector scores highest on the tokens it points toward.


Code
E = model.model.embed_tokens.weight                 # one embedding per vocabulary row
manual = hidden[0, -1].float() @ E.float().T        # dot product with every token's embedding
head = logits[0, -1].float()
diff = (manual - head).abs().max().item()
print(f"logits range from {head.min().item():.1f} to {head.max().item():.1f}")
print(f"largest difference between the two: {diff:.3f}")
assert diff < 0.07 and manual.argmax() == head.argmax()


logits range from -20.0 to 26.6
largest difference between the two: 0.062


The two agree up to rounding. The head stores its logits in bf16, whose spacing near 20 is 0.125, so a difference of up to half that, about 0.06, is just the rounding, and the top token is the same.
Every position gets its own row of logits: position i scores the token that should come at i + 1. For writing an answer only the last position matters, because the prompt is already given. (Training uses all of them; see the chapter on how fine-tuning works.) We check that our step-by-step path reproduces the model’s own forward pass exactly:


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    assert torch.equal(logits, model(input_ids=ids).logits)
last = logits[0, -1].float()
print("scores for the next token:", tuple(last.shape))


scores for the next token: (151936,)




4.2.5 Softmax and the prediction
Logits are arbitrary real numbers. Softmax turns them into probabilities: it exponentiates each score and divides by the total, so every value is positive and they sum to 1.


Code
probs = torch.softmax(last, dim=-1)
best = int(probs.argmax())
gold_id = tok(gold, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"][0]
rank = int((probs > probs[gold_id]).sum()) + 1

print(f"probabilities sum to {probs.sum().item():.4f}")
print(f"most likely next token: {tok.decode([best])!r} with probability {probs[best]:.3f}")
print(f"the gold first token {tok.decode([gold_id])!r}: probability {probs[gold_id]:.3f}, rank {rank}")


probabilities sum to 1.0000
most likely next token: '```' with probability 0.614
the gold first token '5': probability 0.024, rank 5


The untuned model does not know our DSL. It starts a Markdown code block and gives the correct first digit a few percent. Nothing in the pipeline was wrong; the model simply has not seen this task. Teaching it is what fine-tuning does, and we will measure this exact quantity on whole conversations in Chapter 7.


4.2.6 The whole path


Code
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame(
    [
        (
            "token ids",
            tuple(ids.shape),
            "integers from the tokenizer"
        ),
        (
            "embeddings",
            tuple(emb.shape),
            "one learned vector per token"
        ),
        (
            "after 36 layers",
            tuple(hidden.shape),
            "vectors that have read the whole prompt"
        ),

title: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities
text:
4.3 The distribution over next tokens
The softmax output is a whole probability distribution over the vocabulary, not just a winner. Here are the ten most likely next tokens for the prompt above, and how they change with the temperature T: before the softmax, the logits are divided by T.


Code
from convfinqa.book.viz import next_token_stats, plot_next_token

plot_next_token(tok, last, temperatures=(0.3, 1.0, 2.0), k=10);





The ten most likely next tokens at three temperatures.





At T = 1 the logits are used as they are. This is the model’s own distribution.
A low T sharpens it: the leader takes almost everything. As T approaches 0, the result is just the argmax.
A high T flattens it: the tail of unlikely tokens gains probability.

The entropy in the panel titles summarises the spread: it is 0 when one token has all the probability, and grows as the distribution flattens. The same numbers as a table:


Code
pd.DataFrame(
    {f"T = {t}": next_token_stats(last, t, 10) for t in (0.3, 1.0, 2.0)}
).T.round(3)

stats = {t: next_token_stats(last, t, 10) for t in (0.3, 1.0, 2.0)}
gold_id = tok(gold, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids[0]
p_gold = {t: torch.softmax(last.float() / t, dim=-1)[gold_id].item() for t in (1.0, 2.0)}

# the paragraph below

At T = 0.3 the top token holds 99% of the probability. At T = 2 the ten tokens shown hold only 81% of it, and the gold token 5 has more than doubled its probability, from 0.024 to 0.055. The model is not any better informed; the distribution is just less sure of itself.

section: 4.4 Choosing a token: greedy and sampling
text:
4.4 Choosing a token: greedy and sampling
To write more than one token, the model repeats the trace: it picks a token, appends it to the input, and predicts again. How it picks decides everything about the output.

Greedy decoding always takes the most likely token. Nothing is random, so the same input gives the same output.
Sampling draws the next token at random from the (temperature-adjusted) distribution, so the output varies from run to run. A random-number seed makes a sampled run repeatable.

Before we try both, one pitfall. The model ships with default generation settings:


Code
gc = model.generation_config
print({k: getattr(gc, k) for k in ("do_sample", "temperature", "top_p", "top_k")})


{'do_sample': True, 'temperature': 0.7, 'top_p': 0.8, 'top_k': 20}


These are sampling settings, so model.generate() with no arguments samples. Whenever we want greedy decoding we pass do_sample=False explicitly, and for sampling we pass every setting explicitly too.


Code
def continuation(max_new_tokens=14, **kwargs):
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, **kwargs)
    return tok.decode(out[0, ids.shape[1]:])

greedy = dict(do_sample=False, temperature=None, top_p=None, top_k=None)
sampled = dict(do_sample=True, temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0, top_k=0)

rows = [
    ("greedy", "-", continuation(**greedy)),
    ("greedy again", "-", continuation(**greedy))
]
for seed in (0, 1, 2, 0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    rows.append(("sampled", seed, continuation(**sampled)))
assert rows[0][2] == rows[1][2]   # greedy is repeatable
assert rows[2][2] == rows[5][2]   # so is sampling with the same seed

# pandas cuts longer cells at 50 characters
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 80)

pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["decoding", "seed", "first 14 tokens"])

Greedy gives the same text twice. Sampling gives different text for different seeds, and the same text again for the same seed. The untuned model’s greedy answer is not our DSL, but it does contain the right number. It is also the reason this matters later: greedy evaluation is deterministic, so the evaluation chapter has no generation seed to report. Only the training seed varies between runs.


Code
# the same prompt alone and padded inside a batch with a longer one
tok.padding_side = "left"
batch = tok(
    [prompt, prompt + "\nAnswer:"], add_special_tokens=False,
    padding=True, return_tensors="pt"
).to("cuda")
positions = (batch.attention_mask.cumsum(-1) - 1).clamp(min=0)
with torch.no_grad():
    alone = model(ids).logits[0, -1].float()
    together = model(**batch, position_ids=positions).logits[0, -1].float()
batch_diff = (alone - together).abs().max().item()
same_top = alone.argmax() == together.argmax()
print(f"largest change in the logits: {batch_diff:.2f} "
      f"(logits range from {alone.min().item():.0f} to {alone.max().item():.0f}); "
      f"same top token: {bool(same_top)}")
assert batch_diff > 0 and same_top


largest change in the logits: 0.45 (logits range from -20 to 27); same top token: True








NoteDeterministic, but only for the same setup



Greedy decoding is deterministic given the same input, model weights, software and hardware. Running the same prompt inside a different batch can change the logits in bf16, as the check above shows: by up to 0.45 on logits ranging from -20 to 27, with the same top token. That can flip a near-tie. We evaluate with a fixed batch size and a fixed order of examples for this reason.

title: 4  From text to tokens to next-token probabilities
text:
4.5 Editing the logits
A logits processor is a function that edits the logits after the model produces them and before the softmax. The simplest edit is a mask: adding \(-\infty\) to a token’s logit makes its probability exactly 0, and the probabilities of the remaining tokens renormalise to sum to 1.
Say we know the answer to this question is a number, and we allow only the ten digit tokens:


Code
from convfinqa.constrained import AllowedTokens

digit_ids = [
    tok(str(d), add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] for d in range(10)
]
assert all(len(x) == 1 for x in digit_ids)
digit_ids = [x[0] for x in digit_ids]

processor = AllowedTokens(digit_ids)
masked = processor(ids, last[None])[0]
p_masked = torch.softmax(masked, dim=-1)
top = p_masked.topk(3)

print(
    f"P('5') before the mask: {probs[gold_id]:.3f}, after: {p_masked[gold_id]:.3f}"
)
print(
    "top three now:",
    [
        (tok.decode([int(i)]), round(v, 3))
        for v, i in zip(top.values.tolist(), top.indices)
    ]
)


P('5') before the mask: 0.024, after: 0.831
top three now: [('5', 0.831), ('2', 0.164), ('3', 0.002)]


The code fence and program are gone, and the model’s own ranking of the digits decides the rest. Using the processor inside generate:


Code
from transformers import LogitsProcessorList

print(repr(continuation(
    max_new_tokens=4,
    logits_processor=LogitsProcessorList([processor]),
    **greedy
)))


'5363'


The model writes 5363, the gold answer. The mask taught the model nothing: it only removed the options it would have preferred, and the digits it already ranked highest did the rest. That works here because the right answer was already the model’s favourite digit sequence, and it is not guaranteed in general. This mask is also far too crude. It can never end the answer, because the end-of-turn token is not allowed, and it cannot write an operator or a parenthesis. A useful constraint changes the allowed set at every step depending on what has been written so far. That is a grammar, the subject of the constrained-decoding chapter.

title: 5  Anatomy of Qwen3-4B
text:
5.1 Where this architecture comes from
You will learn:
Chapter 4 treated the 36 transformer layers as a black box. This chapter opens it. We start with where the design comes from, because it explains what is, and is not, in the box.
The transformer was introduced for machine translation (Vaswani et al. 2017) as an encoder-decoder, with two stacks:
Qwen3-4B, like most current chat and code models, is decoder-only: one stack with causal self-attention, and no encoder and no cross-attention. The prompt and the answer form a single sequence, and the model’s one job is to predict the next token, as in the trace of Chapter 4.
The ConvFinQA paper’s own model has the traditional shape: a RoBERTa encoder reads the question and the context, and a small recurrent decoder writes the program (Chen et al. 2022).

title: 5  Anatomy of Qwen3-4B
text:
The encoder reads the source sentence. Its self-attention is bidirectional: every position can attend to every other position.
The decoder writes the target sentence one token at a time. Its self-attention is causal: a position sees only the positions before it. Each decoder layer also has a cross-attention block that reads the encoder’s output, which is how the decoder consults the source.




5.1.1 A short history

Decoder-only transformers date from 2018. Liu et al. used one to generate Wikipedia articles from long source documents (Liu et al. 2018), and GPT-1 pretrained one as a language model on unlabeled text, then fine-tuned it for individual tasks (Radford et al. 2018).
GPT-2 (Radford et al. 2019) and GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) scaled the design up. GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, was shown to handle many tasks with no weight updates at all: the task and a few examples are written into the prompt.
Open models later adopted the layout and replaced several of its components (see below). Qwen3 is one of them.



5.1.2 Why decoder-only? What we can say

One objective on plain text. Next-token prediction needs no paired source and target texts, so the same recipe applies to any text.
One model, steered by the prompt. Because the answer continues the prompt, a task can be described in the prompt instead of being built into the architecture (Brown et al. 2020).
Growing prefixes can be reused. Causal attention means a position’s vector never depends on later tokens (we check this on the real model below). When a conversation grows by one turn, the earlier tokens do not need to be recomputed, and a training sequence containing a whole conversation covers every prefix at once. The loss and its gradient on a whole conversation equal the sums over its truncated prefixes; the project’s tests check this numerically on a small model.



5.1.3 What we cannot say
We cannot say that decoder-only is simply better. In a controlled comparison, causal decoder-only models trained autoregressively gave the best zero-shot results after plain pretraining, but models with bidirectional access to the input, trained with masked language modelling and then multitask-finetuned, did best overall (Wang et al. 2022). Encoder-decoder models are still in use. And decoder-only models pay for their simplicity: while reading the prompt, a position cannot use tokens that come after it. This is why our prompts put the page before the question.

title: 5  Anatomy of Qwen3-4B
section: 5.2 What Qwen3-4B keeps from the line, and what it changes
text:
5.2 What Qwen3-4B keeps from the line, and what it changes
The decoder-only layout was refined over the years. The LLaMA paper lists the changes it made to the transformer, crediting each to earlier work (Touvron et al. 2023). We read the implementation of Qwen3 in the Hugging Face library, and it uses the same components, plus one of its own. The Qwen3 report lists the same ones for its dense models, and adds that it removed the bias terms of the attention projections and introduced a normalization of queries and keys for stable training (Yang et al. 2025):




Original transformer
Qwen3-4B




Normalization
LayerNorm after each block
RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019) before each block


Position information
sinusoidal vectors added to the input
rotary embeddings (RoPE) applied inside attention (Su et al. 2021)


Attention heads
every head has its own keys and values
grouped-query attention: 32 query heads share 8 key and value heads (Ainslie et al. 2023)


Feed-forward block
two linear layers with a ReLU
SwiGLU, three linear layers with a gate (Shazeer 2020)


Extra

RMSNorm on every query and key vector



The numbers 32 and 8 come from the model’s config.json, which we read below. The rest of the chapter checks each row against the real model.






Figure 5.1: One decoder-only stack, as in Qwen3-4B: embeddings, 36 identical layers, a final normalization and the output head. Each layer adds an attention update and a feed-forward update to a running sum, shown by the arrows that skip around each block. Position information enters through the attention blocks, not through the embeddings.

title: 5  Anatomy of Qwen3-4B
text:
5.3 Setting up






NoteRequirements



This chapter runs the 4B model on a GPU and reads the artifact conversation_lengths, which Chapter 2 builds. The book is built once by its author, and the executed results are stored in docs/_freeze/, so a reader of the rendered book needs neither.


We load the model and the example from Chapter 4: the first turn of the AAPL conversation, as a prompt whose length is printed below.


Code
import pandas as pd
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages

name = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    name, dtype=torch.bfloat16
).to("cuda").eval()
cfg = model.config

conv = {c["id"]: c for c in data.load_split("train")}\
    ["Single_AAPL/2002/page_23.pdf-1"]

prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
    conversation_messages(conv)[:2],
    tokenize=False,
    add_generation_prompt=True
)

ids = tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False, return_tensors="pt")[
    "input_ids"
].to("cuda")

print("prompt shape:", tuple(ids.shape))


prompt shape: (1, 1125)


To check our explanations against the real model, we record what flows through the first decoder layer. PyTorch lets us attach a hook to any module: a function that is called with the module’s input and output every time it runs. We hook the parts of layer 0, run the prompt once, and keep the tensors in acts.


Code
layer = model.model.layers[0]
parts = {
    "input_layernorm": layer.input_layernorm,
    "q_proj": layer.self_attn.q_proj,
    "k_proj": layer.self_attn.k_proj,
    "v_proj": layer.self_attn.v_proj,
    "q_norm": layer.self_attn.q_norm,
    "k_norm": layer.self_attn.k_norm,
    "o_proj": layer.self_attn.o_proj,
    "self_attn": layer.self_attn,
    "post_attention_layernorm": layer.post_attention_layernorm,
    "gate_proj": layer.mlp.gate_proj,
    "up_proj": layer.mlp.up_proj,
    "down_proj": layer.mlp.down_proj,
    "mlp": layer.mlp,
    "layer": layer,
}
acts = {"token ids": ids}

handles = [layer.register_forward_pre_hook(
    lambda m, args, kwargs: acts.update(layer_input=args[0].detach()),
    with_kwargs=True
)]

for label, module in parts.items():
    handles.append(module.register_forward_hook(
        lambda m, args, out, label=label:
            acts.update({label: (out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out).detach()})
    ))

with torch.no_grad():
    model(input_ids=ids)
for h in handles:
    h.remove()  # later forward passes must not overwrite what we captured


Two small helpers will let each section below show only the model settings and tensor shapes it needs, and a third measures how closely our own calculations match the model’s:


Code
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", None)  # do not cut the meanings short

NOTES = {
    "hidden_size": "length of every token's vector",
    "vocab_size": "rows of the embedding matrix (the tokenizer uses 151,669 of them)",
    "rms_norm_eps": "the ε in RMSNorm",
    "num_attention_heads": "query heads in each attention block",
    "num_key_value_heads": "key and value heads; each serves several query heads",
    "head_dim": "length of one head's query, key and value vectors",
    "rope_theta": "the base Θ of the rotary position angles",
    "attention_bias": "whether the attention projections have bias terms",
    "intermediate_size": "width inside the feed-forward block",
    "hidden_act": "the activation function in the feed-forward block",
    "tie_word_embeddings": "whether the output head reuses the embedding matrix",
}

def show_config(*names):
    """The named settings from the model's config.json, with a short meaning."""
    fmt = (
        lambda v: f"{v:,}"
          if isinstance(v, int) and not isinstance(v, bool)
        else v
    )
    value = (
        lambda n:
            cfg.rope_parameters["rope_theta"]
            if n == "rope_theta"
            else getattr(cfg, n)
    )
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [(fmt(value(n)), NOTES[n]) for n in names],
        index=names,
        columns=["value", "meaning"]
    )

def show_shapes(*items):
    """Shapes of recorded tensors. An item is a key of `acts`,
    or a (label, key) pair.
    """
    pairs = [(i, i) if isinstance(i, str) else i for i in items]
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {"shape": [str(tuple(acts[k].shape)) for _, k in pairs]},
        index=[l for l, _ in pairs]
    )

def rel_err(ours, reference):
    """Largest absolute difference, as a fraction of the largest absolute
    value in the reference.
    """
    return (
        (ours.float() - reference.float()).abs().max()
        / reference.float().abs().max()
    ).item()

title: 5  Anatomy of Qwen3-4B
text:
5.4 The blocks, one by one
In what follows, \(b\) is the sample (batch) index, \(s\) the position in the sequence, and \(h\) the index inside a token’s vector. For each block we list the model settings that determine its size, say what the block does in terms of shapes, and then recompute it by hand from the model’s weights, checking the result against the tensors we recorded. The model computes in bf16, which keeps about three significant digits, so we expect agreement to a fraction of a percent, not bit for bit.

5.4.1 Embedding


Code
show_config("vocab_size", "hidden_size")









value
meaning




vocab_size
151,936
rows of the embedding matrix (the tokenizer uses 151,669 of them)


hidden_size
2,560
length of every token's vector







Embedding takes a tensor of token IDs with shape (batch_size, sequence_length) and maps each token ID to its corresponding embedding vector of size hidden_size, resulting in a tensor of shape (batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_size).


Code
E = model.model.embed_tokens.weight

# the lookup is just indexing rows
assert torch.equal(model.model.embed_tokens(ids), E[ids])

# layer 0 receives the raw embeddings
assert torch.equal(acts["layer_input"], E[ids])

print("embedding matrix:", tuple(E.shape), "(vocab_size, hidden_size)")
show_shapes("token ids", ("embeddings", "layer_input"))


embedding matrix: (151936, 2560) (vocab_size, hidden_size)









shape




token ids
(1, 1125)


embeddings
(1, 1125, 2560)







The second assertion is the point made in the diagram: nothing but the embeddings goes into the first layer. Position information has not been added anywhere yet.


5.4.2 RMSNorm


Code
show_config("rms_norm_eps")









value
meaning




rms_norm_eps
0.000001
the ε in RMSNorm







RMSNorm takes a tensor of shape (batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_size) and normalizes it along the last dimension. If we denote \(b\) as the sample index (1 to batch_size), \(s\) as the sequence index (1 to sequence_length), and \(h\) as the hidden dimension index (1 to hidden_size), then for each element \(x_{b,s,h}\) in the input tensor, RMSNorm computes:
\[
\text{RMSNorm}(x_{b,s,h}) = \frac{x_{b,s,h}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_H} \sum_{h'=1}^{n_H} x_{b,s,h'}^2 + \varepsilon}} \gamma_h
\] where \(n_H\) is hidden_size, \(\gamma_h\) is a learnable weight for the \(h\)-th hidden dimension, and \(\varepsilon\) is a small constant added for numerical stability (Qwen3-4B’s config.json sets it as rms_norm_eps = \(10^{-6}\)).
Each token’s vector is normalized on its own: the sum runs over \(h'\) only, so nothing is mixed across positions or samples. Unlike LayerNorm, there is no mean subtraction; the vector is only rescaled. In code:


Code
def rms_norm(x, weight, eps=cfg.rms_norm_eps):
    return (
        weight.float()
        * (x / torch.sqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + eps))
    )

x = acts["layer_input"].float()

# one RMS per token vector: (batch, tokens, 1)
rms_of = lambda v: v.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True).sqrt()
rms_of_x = rms_of(x)

# broadcast over the hidden dimension, before γ
x_unit_rms = x / rms_of_x
print(
    "RMS of the input vectors:                   ",
    f"{rms_of_x.min().item():.4f} to {rms_of_x.max().item():.4f}"
)
print(
    "Shape of the RMS tensor:                    ",
    f"{rms_of_x.shape}"
)
print(
    "RMS after dividing by it (before scale γ):  ",
    f"{rms_of(x_unit_rms).min().item():.6f} to {rms_of(x_unit_rms).max().item():.6f}"
)

# Compare our RMSNorm implementation with the model's input_layernorm
err = rel_err(rms_norm(x, layer.input_layernorm.weight), acts["input_layernorm"])
print(f"difference from the model's input_layernorm: {err:.4f}")
assert err < 0.02

show_shapes(("input", "layer_input"), ("output", "input_layernorm"))


RMS of the input vectors:                    0.0092 to 0.0253
Shape of the RMS tensor:                     torch.Size([1, 1125, 1])
RMS after dividing by it (before scale γ):   1.000000 to 1.000000
difference from the model's input_layernorm: 0.0045









shape




input
(1, 1125, 2560)


output
(1, 1125, 2560)







The shape does not change. Qwen3 normalizes before each block (“pre-norm”), and applies the same operation on each query and key vector inside attention, with its own learned scale of length head_dim.


5.4.3 Causal self-attention
Attention is the only block in which positions exchange information. The settings that shape it:


Code
show_config(
    "num_attention_heads",
    "num_key_value_heads",
    "head_dim",
    "rope_theta",
    "attention_bias"
)









value

Note that num_attention_heads × head_dim = 32 × 128 = 4,096, which is wider than hidden_size = 2,560. Inside attention the vectors are wider than the running sum, and the output projection brings them back. Figure 5.2 shows the block, and the numbered steps below follow it from the bottom up. Write \(n_Q\) for the number of query heads, \(n_{KV}\) for the number of key/value heads, and \(d\) for head_dim.






Figure 5.2: Inside a causal self-attention block. White boxes hold learned matrices, the green box learned scales, and gray boxes have no learned weights. The shapes beside the arrows use the notation of the text.




Three projections (matrix multiplications, no bias):

\(W_Q\) has dimensions (hidden_size, n_Q*d), with Q = einsum("bsh,hd->bsd", X, W_Q).
\(W_K\) and \(W_V\) have dimensions (hidden_size, n_{KV}*d), with K = einsum("bsh,hd->bsd", X, W_K) and V = einsum("bsh,hd->bsd", X, W_V).

At this point each is one long vector per token, (batch_size, sequence_length, n_Q*d) for \(Q\) and (batch_size, sequence_length, n_KV*d) for \(K\) and \(V\).
Split into heads. Two moves, with no arithmetic. A reshape cuts each long vector into pieces of \(d\) numbers, one per head, giving

(batch_size, sequence_length, n_Q, d) for \(Q\), and
(batch_size, sequence_length, n_KV, d) for \(K\) and \(V\).

A transpose then moves the head index in front of the position index: (batch_size, n_Q, sequence_length, d) and (batch_size, n_KV, sequence_length, d). The diagram shows the result of both moves.
Normalize each query and key vector with RMSNorm over its \(d\) numbers.
Rotate queries and keys by their position. This is rotary position embedding (RoPE), described below.
Share key/value heads. Each key/value head serves \(n_Q / n_{KV}\) consecutive query heads (grouped-query attention), so \(K\) and \(V\) are repeated up to \(n_Q\) heads. Now \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) all have shape (batch_size, n_Q, sequence_length, d).
Score every pair of positions. \(S = QK^\top / \sqrt{d}\) has shape (batch_size, n_Q, sequence_length, sequence_length): entry \((i, j)\) for a given sample and query head is how strongly position \(i\) attends to position \(j\).
Mask the future. Set \(S_{\ldots,ij} = -\infty\) for \(j > i\), so that a position cannot see later ones.
Softmax over \(j\). Each row becomes weights that sum to 1, and the masked entries become exactly 0.
Mix the values and project back. Multiply by \(V\) to get (batch_size, n_Q, sequence_length, d), concatenate the heads into (batch_size, sequence_length, n_Q d), and apply the output projection \(W_O\) to return to hidden_size.

Steps 6 to 8, and the multiplication by \(V\) at the start of step 9, fit in one line. Here \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) are the tensors after steps 1 to 5, and the line is computed separately for each of the \(n_Q\) heads, with the mask \(M\), i.e. \(0\) where \(j \le i\), \(-\infty\) where \(j > i\):
\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}} + M\right) V
\]
Concatenating the heads and applying \(W_O\), the rest of step 9, then turn this into the block’s output.
The shapes recorded from the real layer match the diagram, with one difference in order. The library reshapes the long vectors into heads, (batch, tokens, heads, head_dim), applies q_norm and k_norm there, and only afterwards moves the head index in front of the position index. That is why the recorded shapes of q_norm and k_norm have the heads in the third place. RMSNorm treats each head_dim vector on its own, so the order makes no difference to the result; our code below transposes first, as in the diagram.

5.4.3.1 Rotary position embedding
Take a query or key vector at position \(m\) and split its \(d\) numbers into two halves, \((x_1, x_2)\). For each index \(i\) in the first half, the pair \((x_{1,i}, x_{2,i})\) is rotated by the angle \(\alpha_{m,i} = m\,\theta_i\), where \(\theta_i = \Theta^{-2i/d}\) and \(\Theta\) is rope_theta:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
    x_{1,i}' \\
    x_{2,i}'
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
    \cos\alpha_{m,i} & -\sin\alpha_{m,i} \\
    \sin\alpha_{m,i} & \cos\alpha_{m,i}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
    x_{1,i} \\
    x_{2,i}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
That is, each pair is a point in a plane that is turned about the origin by \(\alpha_{m,i}\).
How the rotation is computed. The rotation matrix is a sum of two simpler pieces,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{pmatrix}
= \cos\alpha \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
+ \sin\alpha \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{J}
\]
where \(J\) turns a vector by 90 degrees: \(J(x_1, x_2) = (-x_2, x_1)\). So the rotated pair is \(\cos\alpha \cdot (x_1, x_2) + \sin\alpha \cdot (-x_2, x_1)\). In the code, rotate_half is \(J\), applied to all \(d/2\) pairs at once (it swaps the two halves of the vector and negates one), and the whole rotation is x * cos + rotate_half(x) * sin, with no matrix built. The tables cos and sin hold one row per position, with each pair’s angle repeated for both halves of the vector so that the products line up.
Why attention sees relative distance. The pairs rotate at different speeds: small \(i\) turns quickly with position, large \(i\) slowly. The useful consequence comes from the fact that rotations compose: turning one vector by \(m\theta_i\) and another by \(n\theta_i\), and taking their dot product, is the same as turning one of them by \((n - m)\theta_i\) and leaving the other alone. So a rotated query at position \(m\) and a rotated key at position \(n\) have a dot product that depends only on the offset \(m - n\), and attention sees relative distance.
We can check this directly. The function rotated_dot rotates a query to position \(m\) and a key to position \(n\), using the formula above, and returns their dot product. It is only a demonstration: the model does the same rotation inside every attention block, and then multiplies queries by keys.


Code
import math

def rope_tables(seq_len, d, theta):
    """For each token position, compute the RoPE angle for each index in
    the head dimension, then return the cosine and sine of those angles.

    The returned cosine and sine tables each have dimension (seq_len, d).
    """
    inv_freq = 1.0\
        / theta ** (torch.arange(0, d, 2, device="cuda").float() / d)
    angles = torch.arange(seq_len, device="cuda")\
        .float()[:, None] * inv_freq[None, :]
    
    # the same angle for both members of a pair
    both = torch.cat([angles, angles], dim=-1)

    return both.cos(), both.sin()

def rotate_half(x):
    """The 90-degree rotation J applied to every pair (x1_i, x2_i):
    (x1, x2) -> (-x2, x1).
    """
    half = x.shape[-1] // 2
    return torch.cat(
        [-x[..., half:], x[..., :half]], dim=-1
    )

d, theta = cfg.head_dim, cfg.rope_parameters["rope_theta"]
cos, sin = rope_tables(ids.shape[1], d, theta)

# one fixed query and one fixed key
torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k = torch.randn(d, device="cuda"), torch.randn(d, device="cuda")

def rotated_dot(m, n):
    """Dot product of the query q rotated to position m and the key k
    rotated to position n.
    """
    # cos(angle) v + sin(angle) J(v)
    rotate = lambda v, pos: v * cos[pos] + rotate_half(v) * sin[pos]
    return (rotate(q, m) @ rotate(k, n)).item()

# Assert that the dot product is consistent for the same offset (seven here),
# regardless of the absolute positions.
dots = [rotated_dot(m + 7, m) for m in (3, 100, 500)]
print("dot products at offset 7:", [round(x, 4) for x in dots])
assert all(math.isclose(x, dots[0], rel_tol=1e-3) for x in dots)


# Compare our cosine table with the library's implementation.
library_cos, _ = model.model.rotary_emb(
    acts["layer_input"],
    torch.arange(ids.shape[1], device="cuda")[None]
)
print(
    "difference from the library's cos table:",
    (cos - library_cos[0].float()).abs().max().item()
)


dot products at offset 7: [18.8659, 18.8659, 18.866]
difference from the library's cos table: 0.001953125


The same query and key give the same dot product at any absolute position, as long as the offset is the same. Our tables also agree with the library’s, up to the library storing them in bf16.


5.4.3.2 One full attention block
We now implement the whole attention block, step by step as listed above:


Code
def attention(x, attn, cos, sin):
    """x: (batch, seq, hidden), already normalized.
    Returns a tensor of shape (batch, seq, hidden).
    """
    b, s, _ = x.shape
    n_q = cfg.num_attention_heads
    n_kv = cfg.num_key_value_heads
    d = cfg.head_dim

    # w -> w^T (project input using weight matrix)
    project = lambda w: x @ w.weight.float().T

    # Project input to query, key, and value spaces using the respective weight matrices,
    # then reshape and transpose into (batch, heads, seq, head_dim) format.
    q = project(attn.q_proj).view(b, s, n_q, d).transpose(1, 2)    # (b, n_q, s, d)
    k = project(attn.k_proj).view(b, s, n_kv, d).transpose(1, 2)   # (b, n_kv, s, d)
    v = project(attn.v_proj).view(b, s, n_kv, d).transpose(1, 2)

    # Apply RMS normalization to the queries and keys.
    q, k = rms_norm(q, attn.q_norm.weight), rms_norm(k, attn.k_norm.weight)

    # Apply rotary positional embeddings to the queries and keys.
    q, k = q * cos + rotate_half(q) * sin, k * cos + rotate_half(k) * sin

    # Repeat K and V to match the number of query heads.
    k = k.repeat_interleave(n_q // n_kv, dim=1)
    v = v.repeat_interleave(n_q // n_kv, dim=1)

    # Compute attention scores.
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(d)  # (b, n_q, s, s)

    # Create the causal mask for future positions.
    future = torch.triu(
        torch.ones(s, s, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device),
        diagonal=1
    )
    # Apply the causal mask to the attention scores, then compute the softmax
    # to get attention weights.
    weights = torch.softmax(
        scores.masked_fill(future, float("-inf")), dim=-1
    )

    # Compute the weighted sum of values using the attention weights.
    mixed = (weights @ v).transpose(1, 2)\
        .reshape(b, s, n_q * d)  # heads side by side
    
    # Project the mixed output back to the hidden dimension using
    # the output projection.
    return mixed @ attn.o_proj.weight.float().T


# Compute the output of the attention block (one RMSNorm and one attention layer)
normed = rms_norm(acts["layer_input"].float(), layer.input_layernorm.weight)
attn_out = attention(normed, layer.self_attn, cos, sin)

# Compare the computed attention output with the model's stored
# self-attention output
err = rel_err(attn_out, acts["self_attn"])
print(f"difference from the model's self_attn output: {err:.4f}")
assert err < 0.02


difference from the model's self_attn output: 0.0035




5.4.3.3 The mask in action
Because of the mask in step 7, the vector at each position depends only on the tokens up to and including it. We check this on the whole model: replace the last 200 tokens of the prompt with a different token, and compare the final vectors.


Code
cut = ids.shape[1] - 200

# Create a modified version of the input with the last 200 tokens changed
changed = ids.clone()
changed[0, cut:] = tok("x", add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"][0]

# Compute the model's final hidden states (after all 36 layers) for both the
# original and modified inputs (shape: (seq_length, hidden_size))
with torch.no_grad():
    before = model.model(input_ids=ids).last_hidden_state[0].float()
    after = model.model(input_ids=changed).last_hidden_state[0].float()

# Compare the hidden states before and after the change
print(
    "positions before the change, largest difference:",
    (before[:cut] - after[:cut]).abs().max().item()
)
print(
    "positions after the change, largest difference: ",
    (before[cut:] - after[cut:]).abs().max().item()
)
assert (before[:cut] - after[:cut]).abs().max().item() < 1e-2


positions before the change, largest difference: 0.0
positions after the change, largest difference:  130.25


The first 925 positions are untouched, even after 36 layers, and only the replaced ones change. This is why earlier tokens never need to be recomputed when a conversation grows, and why a whole conversation can be trained in one pass.



5.4.4 Feed-forward block
After attention has mixed information across positions, the feed-forward network (FFN) processes each position on its own, with the same weights at every position. The library calls it mlp, so that is the name we will see in the code. Its settings:


Code
show_config("intermediate_size", "hidden_act")









value
meaning




intermediate_size
9,728
width inside the feed-forward block


hidden_act
silu
the activation function in the feed-forward block







It takes (batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_size) and returns the same shape, passing through a wider space of size intermediate_size (written \(i\) in Figure 5.3):






Figure 5.3: Inside the feed-forward block. Two matrices widen the vector; the SiLU of one acts as a gate on the other, and the product is narrowed back to the hidden size.



\[
\text{FFN}(x) = W_{\text{down}}\Big(\operatorname{SiLU}(x W_{\text{gate}}) \odot (x W_{\text{up}})\Big),
\qquad \operatorname{SiLU}(z) = z \cdot \sigma(z)
\]
where \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid and \(\odot\) multiplies element by element. \(W_{\text{gate}}\) and \(W_{\text{up}}\) widen the vector from hidden_size to intermediate_size; the SiLU of the first acts as a soft gate on the second, deciding how much of each wide feature passes; and \(W_{\text{down}}\) narrows the result back. The original transformer used two matrices and a ReLU; this three-matrix gated form is called SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020).
The split paths of Figure 5.3, where two projections of the same input are multiplied, have been found empirically to give better results than a plain dense layer followed by an activation (Shazeer 2020). There is no settled explanation for why.


Code
def ffn(x, mlp):
    gate = torch.nn.functional.silu(x @ mlp.gate_proj.weight.float().T)
    up = x @ mlp.up_proj.weight.float().T
    return (gate * up) @ mlp.down_proj.weight.float().T

# Input to the second half of the layer (the feed-forward half)
h1 = acts["layer_input"].float() + acts["self_attn"].float()

# Apply RMSNorm before feeding into the feed-forward block,
# then compare it to the model's output for the feed-forward block
normed = rms_norm(h1, layer.post_attention_layernorm.weight)
err = rel_err(ffn(normed, layer.mlp), acts["mlp"])
print(f"difference from the model's mlp output: {err:.4f}")
assert err < 0.02

5.4.5 Residual connections and one whole layer
Neither block replaces its input. Each one adds its result to it, which is the residual connection drawn as the loops in Figure 5.1. With \(x\) the layer’s input:
\[
h = x + \text{Attention}\big(\text{RMSNorm}(x)\big),
\qquad
y = h + \text{FFN}\big(\text{RMSNorm}(h)\big)
\]
The output \(y\) has the same shape as \(x\) and goes to the next layer. Our functions are enough to reproduce a whole layer:


Code
def decoder_layer(x, layer, cos, sin):
    """Apply one decoder layer to the input x.
    
    First, the input goes through the attention block with a residual connection,
    then through the feed-forward block with another residual connection.
    """
    x = x + attention(
        rms_norm(x, layer.input_layernorm.weight),
        layer.self_attn,
        cos,
        sin
    )
    return x + ffn(
        rms_norm(x, layer.post_attention_layernorm.weight),
        layer.mlp
    )

# Compare the output of our decoder layer with the model's output
err = rel_err(
    decoder_layer(acts["layer_input"].float(), layer, cos, sin),
    acts["layer"]
)
print(f"difference from the model's layer 0 output: {err:.4f}")
assert err < 0.02

5.4.6 Linear output head
After the last layer, one more RMSNorm, then the output head: a matrix multiplication that turns each position’s vector of hidden_size numbers into vocab_size scores, the logits. For a vector \(y\) and the embedding matrix \(E\) of shape (vocab_size, hidden_size):
\[
\text{logits} = \text{RMSNorm}(y)\, E^\top
\]
because in this model the head and the embedding matrix are the same tensor (as seen in the previous chapter):

We have now met every part of the model. Here it is as the library prints it; PyTorch collapses the 36 identical layers into one entry, and every name in it is a block from the sections above.

          (gate_proj): Linear(in_features=2560, out_features=9728, bias=False)
          (up_proj): Linear(in_features=2560, out_features=9728, bias=False)
          (down_proj): Linear(in_features=9728, out_features=2560, bias=False)

Run the embeddings through all 36 layers with our functions, then the final norm and the head, and compare the prediction with the model’s:

with torch.no_grad():
    x = model.model.embed_tokens.weight[ids].float()
    for each_layer in model.model.layers:
        x = decoder_layer(x, each_layer, cos, sin)
    x = rms_norm(x, model.model.norm.weight)
    ours = x[0, -1] @ model.model.embed_tokens.weight.float().T
    theirs = model(input_ids=ids).logits[0, -1].float()

def top(logits, k=5):
    p = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1).topk(k)
    return [
        (tok.decode([int(i)]), round(v, 3))
        for v, i in zip(p.values.tolist(), p.indices)
    ]

print("ours:  ", top(ours))
print("model: ", top(theirs))
assert int(ours.argmax()) == int(theirs.argmax())

5.6 Counting parameters and memory
Every number in the model is a parameter in one of the matrices or vectors above, so we can count them from the shapes and check the total against PyTorch’s count.

per_layer = {
    "attention: q, k, v, o projections": sum(
        m.weight.numel()
        for m in (at.q_proj, at.k_proj, at.v_proj, at.o_proj)
    ),
    "feed-forward: gate, up, down": sum(
        m.weight.numel()
        for m in (ml.gate_proj, ml.up_proj, ml.down_proj)
    ),

        w.numel()
        for w in (

}
