Code
fp32, bf16 = checks["fp32"], checks["bf16"]
assert fp32["merge_max_abs_diff"] < 0.01 * fp32["adapter_effect_max_abs"]\
    and fp32["merge_top1_agreement"] == 1.0


In fp32, merging is the same function. The largest difference between the merged and the separate adapter is 0.002 in the logits, against 14.7 for the effect of the adapter itself, and the top token is the same at every position: the difference is float rounding.
In bf16, it is not. The largest difference is 15.3, as large as the adapter’s own effect, and the merged model picks a different top token at 4% of the positions. One likely reason: the merged weights \(W + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\) are rounded to bf16 when they are stored, which discards the low bits of a small correction, and the separate adapter keeps them. Another is probably that a random \(B\) is a large, arbitrary perturbation of the model, which makes its output sensitive to every small rounding, so a trained adapter, smaller and with structure, may merge better. We have not measured that.
What does keep the adapter’s exact effect is not to merge it into bf16 weights: either leave it separate, a bf16 base model with an fp32 adapter, which is how we train it and PEFT’s default, or merge and keep the whole model in fp32 (twice the memory). Merging and then casting to bf16 stores rounded weights, which is the case we measured, so a merged bf16 model has to be evaluated before it is relied on. Chapter 13 does that on the trained adapter.

title: 9  LoRA in detail
section: 9.5 Rank, alpha and what we leave out
text:
9.5 Rank, alpha and what we leave out

Rank is capacity: a rank-\(r\) update can change each layer’s output in only \(r\) directions. Too small and the model cannot fit the task; beyond what the task needs, more rank only adds weights. How much the task needs is an empirical question, and we answer it with a rank sweep, below and above 16 (Chapter 17).
Alpha sets the size of the correction. Keeping \(\alpha = 2r\) keeps the scale fixed at 2 whatever the rank, so rank is the only thing the sweep changes.
QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) stores the frozen base weights in 4 bits, to save memory, and trains the adapters in higher precision on top. We do not need it: the 4B model’s bf16 weights take 8 GB, which the machine holds with room to spare.







NoteUnder the hood



The two views of Figure 9.1 compute the same function in exact arithmetic, but they are not interchangeable in practice. Training runs the right-hand view, because it never builds the big matrix. Merging builds \(W + \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\) once, which is what makes inference free of extra cost. A merge cannot be undone exactly: once the correction is added to bf16 weights the original \(W\) cannot be recovered, so we keep the adapter file and not only the merged model. In fp32 the adapter of the main run is about 132 MB, against 8 GB for the model.








TipFurther reading




The LoRA paper (Hu et al. 2022) introduces the method and the low-rank hypothesis it rests on.
QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) combines it with a 4-bit base model.
Low-rank factorization for recommendation (Koren et al. 2009) is the older use of the same product-of-thin-matrices idea.









Dettmers, Tim, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, and Luke Zettlemoyer. 2023. “QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36.


Hu, Edward J., Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, et al. 2022. “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations.


Koren, Yehuda, Robert Bell, and Chris Volinsky. 2009. “Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems.” Computer 42 (8): 30–37.

title: 10  Formatting conversations for training
text:
10.1 The messages
You will learn:
Chapter 6 explained chat templates and teacher forcing in general. This chapter fixes the format we use for ConvFinQA, shows it on a real conversation, and checks the properties the later chapters rely on. Nothing here trains a model: it prepares the data that the training and evaluation chapters read.
A conversation becomes one chat. A fixed system message comes first. The first user message holds the page, that is the text before the table, the table as markdown and the text after it, followed by the first question. The assistant’s reply is the gold program for that turn. Each later turn adds a user message with the question alone, and the assistant’s reply with its gold program. formatting.conversation_messages does this. Here it is on a validation conversation with three turns:
Code
from IPython.display import HTML, display

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.artifacts import get
from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages

val = list(get("train_val_split").jsonl("val.jsonl"))
three = [c for c in val if len(c["annotation"]["turn_program"]) == 3]
conv = min(
    three,
    key=lambda c: sum(len(p) for p in c["annotation"]["turn_program"])
)
messages = conversation_messages(conv)

def short(text, head=110, tail=60):
    text = text.replace("\n", " ⏎ ")
    return (
        text if len(text) <= head + tail + 5
        else text[:head] + " … " + text[-tail:]
    )

print(conv["id"], f"(Type {data.conversation_type(conv)})\n")
for m in messages:
    print(f"{m['role']:>9}: {short(m['content'])}")


Double_ADBE/2003/page_90.pdf (Type II)

   system: Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL.
     user: building . the construction of the building was completed in december 2003 . due to lower than expected financ … ating leases net of sublease income due in less than 1 year?
assistant: 23.6
     user: what about the total non-cancelable operating leases net of sublease income?
assistant: 83.9
     user: what portion is due in less than 1 year?
assistant: divide(23.6, 83.9)
The page appears once, in the first user message, because it does not change. The later questions refer to it and to the earlier answers, as a real conversation would.

title: 10  Formatting conversations for training
text:
10.2 What the loss counts
The messages are turned into token ids by the model’s chat template, and a second list, the labels, says which of those tokens the model is trained to produce. A label is the token id where the token counts and -100 where it does not (Chapter 8 showed why the value is -100). The rule is simple: only the assistant’s answers count, together with the <|im_end|> token that ends each one. Figure 10.1 shows the layout.






Figure 10.1: Two ways to lay out the training data for a conversation of three turns (not to scale: the page is the long part). One sequence per conversation reads the page once and trains all three answers. One sequence per turn trains the same three answers, but reads the page and the earlier answers again for every turn.



On our conversation, with the first part of the sequence cut off, the tokens look like this. Green tokens are trained, grey ones are only read:


Code
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

from convfinqa.book.viz import trained_html
from convfinqa.formatting import tokenize_conversation

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")
ids, labels = tokenize_conversation(tok, messages)
first = next(i for i, label in enumerate(labels) if label != -100)
start = first - 40  # the end of the first user message, and everything after it
pieces = [tok.decode([i]) for i in ids[start:]]
display(HTML(
    '<div style="opacity:0.7">… (the first ' + f"{start:,}"
    + " tokens: the system message and the page)</div>"
    + trained_html(pieces, [label != -100 for label in labels[start:]])
))
print(
    f"{len(ids):,} tokens in all, "
    f"{sum(label != -100 for label in labels)} of them trained"
)

How much of a sequence is trained? We can count over the whole validation split, and check that the count is the one the untuned model’s loss was measured on in Chapter 7:


Code
print(
    "the template has generation markers:",
    "{% generation %}" in tok.chat_template
)

total = trained = 0
for c in val:
    ids_c, labels_c = tokenize_conversation(tok, conversation_messages(c))
    total += len(ids_c)
    trained += sum(label != -100 for label in labels_c)
share = trained / total
print(f"validation split: {total:,} tokens, {trained:,} trained ({share:.1%})")

# the count the untuned loss was measured on
assert trained == get("val_gold_nll").json("nll.json")["tokens"]


the template has generation markers: False
validation split: 347,006 tokens, 16,417 trained (4.7%)


Three details of the layout:

The answers are green, the markers around them are not. The model is given <|im_start|>assistant and the newline that follows it, so these are grey: they are the generation prompt of the next section. It is asked to produce the answer and the <|im_end|> after it, which is how it learns to stop. The newline that the template writes after <|im_end|> is grey too.
Most of the sequence is not trained. The page and the questions are many tokens, and the answers few. Over the whole validation split the answers are 4.7% of the tokens.
The labels are ours. The chat template of this model has no {% generation %} markers, which is what TRL’s assistant_only_loss option needs. We do not need them: tokenize_conversation renders the chat up to each assistant message and finds the answer’s tokens itself, and the Trainer uses a labels column as it is.

title: 10  Formatting conversations for training
text:
10.3 One sequence per conversation
Why is it allowed to train on all the answers of a conversation in one pass? Because the model is causal: the output at a position depends only on the tokens before it. The loss on the answer of turn \(k\) therefore depends only on the tokens up to that answer, exactly as if the sequence had ended there. The summed loss of the whole conversation is the sum of the losses of the truncated sequences, and so is its gradient. tests/test_causal_prefix.py checks both on a small Qwen3, and also checks the limit of the claim: only the end of a conversation can be cut, because removing early tokens changes every later loss. Two training runs, one in each layout, are therefore equivalent up to batching (a step of 16 conversations holds far more answer tokens than a step of 16 turns) and rounding (different padding and batching change bf16 results), but not step for step.
The saving is the one counted in Chapter 6: the per-turn layout of Figure 10.1 reads several times as many tokens for the same answers. The price is the one named there too, exposure bias: during training every earlier answer in the context is the gold one.


Code
lengths = get("conversation_lengths").json("lengths.json")
assert lengths["longest"] <= lengths["max_length"]


Nothing is cut by max_length: the longest full conversation of the data is 3,460 tokens (Chapter 2) and max_length is 3,584.

title: 10  Formatting conversations for training
text:
10.4 Train, validation and dev
train.json is the training file. We hold out a tenth of its conversations as validation data, for the choices that the project makes (the prompt, the checkpoint, the grammar) and train on the rest. Several conversations are written from the same report page, so the split is made by page: the group key is the conversation id without its Single_ or Double_ prefix and its -N suffix. A page then lies entirely on one side, and the model is never scored on a page it trained on.


Code

fit = list(get("train_val_split").jsonl("train_fit.jsonl"))
dev = data.load_split("dev")

n_turns = lambda convs: sum(len(c["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) for c in convs)
sizes = pd.DataFrame({
    "conversations": {
        "train-fit": len(fit),
        "val": len(val),
        "dev": len(dev)
    },

        "train-fit": n_turns(fit),
        "val": n_turns(val),
        "dev": n_turns(dev)
    },

        "train-fit": len(pages(fit)),
        "val": len(pages(val)),
        "dev": len(pages(dev))

})

print(
    f"dev pages that also occur in train: "
    f"{len(pages(dev) & (pages(fit) | pages(val)))} of {len(pages(dev))}"

title: 10  Formatting conversations for training
text:
10.5 Prompts for evaluation
At evaluation time the model sees the conversation up to the question of turn \(k\), and writes the answer. The prompt is the training sequence cut right before that answer, with the generation prompt at the end. formatting.prompt_messages builds the chat. Earlier answers are the gold programs by default (the gold history of the evaluation chapters). The model’s own earlier answers can be passed instead (the predicted history), and complete example conversations can be put in front (few-shot):


Code
from convfinqa.formatting import prompt_messages

def outline(chat):
    return " | ".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content'][:24]}…" for m in chat)

print("gold history, turn 3:\n ", outline(prompt_messages(conv, 2)), "\n")
print(
    "predicted history, turn 3:\n ",
    outline(prompt_messages(
        conv, 2, history=["(the model's answer 1)", "(the model's answer 2)"]
    )),
    "\n"
)
print(
    "one example first, turn 3 (s = system, u = user, a = assistant):\n ",
    " ".join(m["role"][0] for m in prompt_messages(conv, 2, examples=[fit[0]]))
)

  system: Answer with a program in… | user: building . the construct… | assistant: 23.6… | user: what about the total non… | assistant: 83.9… | user: what portion is due in l… 

predicted history, turn 3:
  system: Answer with a program in… | user: building . the construct… | assistant: (the model's answer 1)… | user: what about the total non… | assistant: (the model's answer 2)… | user: what portion is due in l…

What the model reads in training and in evaluation must be the same, token for token, or the evaluation measures a different task from the one trained. We can check it on every turn of the validation split: the tokens of the prompt for turn \(k\) must be the training sequence up to where the answer of turn \(k\) begins.


Code
def answer_starts(labels):
    return [
        i for i, label in enumerate(labels)
        if label != -100
        and (i == 0 or labels[i - 1] == -100)
    ]

checked = 0
for c in val:
    ids_c, labels_c = tokenize_conversation(tok, conversation_messages(c))
    starts = answer_starts(labels_c)
    assert len(starts) == len(data.turns(c))
    for k, s in enumerate(starts):
        prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
            prompt_messages(c, k), tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True
        )
        assert tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] == ids_c[:s]
        checked += 1
print(
    f"{checked:,} prompts checked: each is the training sequence up to the "
    "start of its answer"
)


1,125 prompts checked: each is the training sequence up to the start of its answer

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.1 What we measure
You will learn:
Fine-tuning will be judged by what it adds to the model we start from, so before training anything we measure what Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 already does on ConvFinQA. The comparison is only worth making if the baseline is a fair one. A weak prompt would make any later improvement look bigger than it is. So the untuned model gets the best help we can give it without changing its weights: a description of the DSL, and complete example conversations written into the prompt (Brown et al. 2020).
For every turn of a conversation, the model reads a prompt and writes a program. Our executor runs the program, and the result is compared with the gold answer: this is execution accuracy, and an output that does not run counts as wrong. The prompt for turn \(k\) ends with question \(k\), and what comes before it depends on how the earlier answers are supplied (Chapter 10):
Chapter 6 explained why the two differ: teacher forcing, and exposure bias.

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
with the gold history, every earlier answer in the prompt is the dataset’s own program, so each turn is scored on its own;
with the predicted history, they are the model’s own earlier outputs, mistakes included, and errors compound from turn to turn. This is the setting a real user would meet, and the one we treat as the headline.

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.2 What to expect
The ConvFinQA paper found that an unfamiliar program syntax hurt GPT-3 (Chen et al. 2022), and in Chapter 7 the untuned model’s errors were mostly failures of format: prose, or arithmetic in other notations, instead of a program. So a good part of what the examples and the description can fix is the format. Choosing the right operation and numbers is the other part, and it is the one we expect fine-tuning to have to teach.

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.3 How the experiment is organised

Prompts. A prompt holds the system message, then the example set (complete training conversations, written as earlier turns of the chat), then the target conversation up to the current question. The system message is a single line, or the same line plus a compact description of the DSL and the rule that an answer is a program and nothing else, or that plus a rule against nested calls.
Example sets. Which examples are used changes the result, and an untuned model has no training seed to vary, so the examples play that part. An example set is fixed by its seed alone, so the same seed gives the same examples whichever data we evaluate on. Three sets are prepared, and the reported baseline uses the first (seed 0): one run, with the uncertainty of its accuracy taken from the paired bootstrap, which covers the choice of report pages and not the choice of examples.
Choosing the prompt. The variants we try (how many examples, with or without the description, and none at all) are listed in advance (one more was added after the first results, and is flagged), and the choice between them is made on the validation data. The development data are touched only for the numbers the book reports, once, with the prompt already chosen.
Scoring. Generation and scoring are separate steps, so the measures can be refined without generating again. This chapter uses execution accuracy, and counts how the invalid outputs fail; the other measures are introduced later, where they are used.

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.4 The experiment, exactly

11.4.1 The prompt
Figure 11.1 shows one prompt, and the three runs that the example sets make.






Figure 11.1: The baseline’s prompt (left) and its runs (right). The system message and the examples are the same in every prompt of a run, and the target conversation changes with every turn. Each run uses one example set; the reported baseline is one run.



The system message has three forms. The plain one is the line the models are trained with, Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL. The second adds a description of the language and the rule that the answer is the program and nothing else. Its text is fixed now, and is not tuned on the validation data:
Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL, and write nothing else: no explanation and no code block.

A program is a single number, or a list of steps separated by ", ":
    operation(argument, argument)
The operations are add, subtract, multiply, divide, exp and greater (greater gives yes or no).
An argument is one of:
    a number copied from the page, without thousands separators (a percentage keeps its % sign);
    #k, the result of step k, counting steps from 0;
    a constant: const_1 to const_9, const_10, const_100 and so on up to const_1000000000, or const_m1 for -1.
The third form, flat, was added after the first six variants had been run, because their errors showed a pattern (see the results below). It is the description plus one rule, with a made-up example of the contrast:
Each step holds exactly one operation, and an argument is never another operation: write every calculation as a step
of its own and refer back to it with #k. For example, write "subtract(5, 3), divide(#0, 3)", never
"divide(subtract(5, 3), 3)".
The examples are 2 or 3 complete conversations from train-fit, written as earlier turns of the chat, as in Chapter 10. A set of examples is built from a seeded shuffle of train-fit, position by position: a Type I conversation, then a Type II one, then another Type I. A set therefore holds exactly one Type II conversation, and the two-example prompt (the first two) shows one of each kind; it is a prefix of the three-example one. The seeds are 0, 1 and 2, fixed in advance, and no two examples, in a set or between sets, come from the same report page (several conversations are written from one page, so two of them would show the same table twice). The sets are saved, as lists of conversation ids, so that a run can be checked against them.


11.4.2 The variants, and the choice
Seven prompts were compared on the validation data. Those with examples use the first example set (seed 0), taking its first two or three examples as indicated; those with no examples have no set. Each prompt is a single run. Sets 1 and 2 were prepared for the reported runs on the development data and are not used: the freeze limits those runs to set 0.










one-line system message
with the description
description and the flat rule




no examples
e0p
e0d



2 examples
e2p
e2d



3 examples
e3p
e3d
e3f (added afterwards)



e3f is post-hoc: it was thought of after reading the errors of the six, so it is flagged as such wherever it appears, and the other prompts of its kind (e0f, e2f) are not run.
The seven prompts are scored with the predicted history, the headline setting. One of them becomes the untuned baseline: the prompt that is run on the development data and that the fine-tuned models are compared with. It is chosen on the validation data by a rule that was written down before the first six were run, and applied unchanged to the seventh:

find the variant with the highest execution accuracy;
keep every variant that it does not clearly beat, that is, whose paired bootstrap interval for the best variant’s lead includes zero (the best variant itself is always kept);
among those, take the one with the fewest examples, and then the plain system message before the description.

Only clear differences count: the rule works on the paired intervals, which are narrower than the intervals of the accuracies themselves (the table below shows how wide those are).


11.4.3 The runs that are reported
The chosen variant is then run on the development data, once, after the decisions of the project are frozen: with the first example set, in each of the two history modes. Both modes are scored on the same predictions of the same prompts, which differ only in how the earlier answers are filled in.
One more prompt is run on the development data whatever the choice: e0p, the one-line message with no examples. It is exactly what the fine-tuned model will be given, so comparing the two shows what the training changed, with the input held fixed. It plays no part in the choice of the baseline.
Figure 11.2 shows the difference between the two modes in how the runs are organised.






Figure 11.2: The two history modes on four conversations of one to four turns. With the gold history, every turn is its own prompt, and all ten can be built in advance and run in any order. With the predicted history, a round asks every conversation that has reached turn k, and the model’s answers to earlier turns enter the prompts of the next round.





11.4.4 Generation


Code
import json
from pathlib import Path

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

from convfinqa import data
from convfinqa.artifacts import get

max_new = json.loads(Path("../configs/baseline.json").read_text())["max_new_tokens"]
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")
split = get("train_val_split")
gold_longest = max(
    len(tok(t.program).input_ids)
    for name in ("train_fit.jsonl", "val.jsonl")
    for c in split.jsonl(name)
    for t in data.turns(c)
)
assert max_new >= 1.5 * gold_longest  # clearly above, so no program is cut


Decoding is greedy and stops at the end-of-turn token or after 96 new tokens, which is above the longest gold program (64 tokens, over train-fit and validation). Prompts are run one at a time: with prompts this long the model spends its time reading, so batching gains little, and a prompt’s output then cannot depend on which other prompts share its batch (bf16 results change slightly with the batch). An output that reaches the limit is scored as written. Every prediction is stored with the conversation id, the turn, the text, the number of tokens and why generation stopped, and scoring reads these files, so the measures can change without generating again.


11.4.5 Scoring
The measure is execution accuracy: the executor of Chapter 3 runs the output, and the result is compared with the gold answer. An output that does not run counts as wrong. Alongside it we count the invalid outputs by cause, with the kinds of Chapter 7, and the ones that write a calculation as a nested call. More measures (how closely the program matches the gold one, how numbers are written, answers off by a power of ten, accuracy by turn and by conversation type) are defined in the chapter that evaluates the fine-tuned models, where they are used on every system at once. The stored predictions are enough to compute them for the baseline without generating again.

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.5 The code
Three artifacts carry the experiment. example_sets is light: it draws the sets from the ids of train-fit, and is saved so that nothing depends on how the random draw behaves in a later version of Python. The two others are named by the split, the prompt variant, the example-set seed and the history mode. untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode} loads the model and writes one prediction per turn; its development on dev is refused until a configs/FROZEN file exists, which is how the freeze of the data protocol is enforced. scores_untuned_… is light: it executes and scores the predictions.


Code
from convfinqa.artifacts import artifact, get


@artifact(
    "untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=["train_val_split", "eval_turns", "example_sets"],
    files=["configs/baseline.json"],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_untuned(
    out, deps, files, *, split: str, variant: str, seed: int, mode: str
):
    import json
    import time

    from convfinqa.evaluate import (
        load_model, make_generator, require_freeze, run_generation
    )
    from convfinqa.prompts import parse_variant

    require_freeze(split)
    cfg = files["configs/baseline.json"].json()
    n_examples, kind = parse_variant(variant)
    if n_examples == 0 and seed != 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "a variant with no examples has no example set: use seed 0"
        )
    if split == "val":
        convs = list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl"))
    elif split == "dev":
        convs = list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl"))
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"split must be 'val' or 'dev', not {split!r}")
    examples = []
    if n_examples:
        wanted = deps["example_sets"].json("sets.json")\
            ["sets"][str(seed)][:n_examples]
        pool = {
            c["id"]: c
            for c in deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("train_fit.jsonl")
        }
        examples = [pool[i] for i in wanted]

    model, tok = load_model(cfg["model"], cfg["memory_cap_gb"])
    generate = make_generator(model, tok, cfg["max_new_tokens"])
    start, done = time.perf_counter(), 0
    with open(out / "predictions.jsonl", "w") as f:
        def sink(row):
            nonlocal done
            f.write(json.dumps({
                k: v for k, v in row.items() if k != "seconds"
            }) + "\n")   # timing is not an output
            f.flush()
            done += 1
            if done % 50 == 0:
                print(
                    f"{done} turns, {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s",
                    flush=True
                )

        run_generation(
            convs, generate, system=cfg["system"][kind],
            examples=examples, mode=mode, sink=sink
        )
    print(f"done: {done} turns in {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s")


@artifact(
    "scores_untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=["untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}", "eval_turns"],
)
def build_scores_untuned(
    out, deps, *, split: str, variant: str, seed: int, mode: str
):
    import json

    from convfinqa.evaluate import score_rows, summarize
    from convfinqa.program_match import add_program_match

    rows = list(
        deps[f"untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}"]
        .jsonl("predictions.jsonl")
    )
    turns = list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl"))
    scores = add_program_match(score_rows(rows, turns), rows, turns)
    (out / "scores.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(s) + "\n" for s in scores)
    )
    (out / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(summarize(scores), indent=2)
    )

title: 11  The untuned baseline
text:
11.6 Choosing the prompt
The seven prompts, on the validation data, with the predicted history. Each accuracy comes with a 95% confidence interval, found by resampling whole report pages, with every conversation written from them (not single turns: the turns of one conversation, and the conversations written from one page, are not independent). The scores are read from the prediction files.


Code
#HEAVY
import pandas as pd

from convfinqa.baseline_report import choose_variant, comparison_rows
from convfinqa.prompts import VARIANTS
from convfinqa.stats import paired_difference

scores = {
    v: list(get(f"scores_untuned_val_{v}_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl"))
    for v in VARIANTS
}
predictions = {
    v: list(get(f"untuned_val_{v}_0_pred").jsonl("predictions.jsonl"))
    for v in VARIANTS
}
rows = {r["variant"]: r for r in comparison_rows(scores, predictions)}
pct = lambda x: f"{100 * x:.1f}%"
pts = lambda x: f"{100 * x:+.1f}"
diff = lambda a, b: paired_difference(scores[a], scores[b])

pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "variant": v + (" (post-hoc)" if v.endswith("f") else ""),
        "execution accuracy":
            f"{pct(r['accuracy'])} [{pct(r['low'])}, {pct(r['high'])}]",
        "invalid outputs": r["invalid"],
        "of which nested": f"{r['nested']} ({r['nested_share']:.0%})",
        "prompt tokens": f"{r['prompt_tokens']:.0f}",
    }
    for v, r in rows.items()

#HEAVY
widths = [
    100 * (r["high"] - r["low"])
    for v, r in rows.items()

With examples, the confidence interval of each accuracy is 8 to 8 percentage points wide, so two prompts whose accuracies differ by a point or two cannot be told apart from the two intervals alone. The comparison between prompts is paired (both are scored on the same conversations), which is why it can resolve smaller differences, as the rule of Section 11.4.2 does.
The rule defined in Section 11.4.2 is applied in code, not by eye:


Code
#HEAVY
choice = choose_variant(scores)
best, chosen = choice["best"], choice["chosen"]
assert chosen == "e3p"   # the prose below describes this outcome


The best accuracy is e3p’s, at 57.2%. Table 11.1 shows its lead over each other variant, as a difference in accuracy with its paired confidence interval. The variants that it does not clearly beat (the interval includes zero) are e3p, e3d, e3f, so the rule picks e3p: among equals, the plain message.

    }
    for v, d in choice["leads"].items()
]).set_index("variant")

#HEAVY
half = [
    100 * (d["high"] - d["low"]) / 2
    for v, d in choice["leads"].items()
    if not v.startswith("e0")
]

# a paired interval is narrower than that of an accuracy
assert max(half) < 4 and min(half) > 1

overlap = [
    v for v, d in choice["leads"].items()
    if d["excludes_zero"] and rows[v]["high"] > rows[best]["low"]
]

# some leads are clear although the two accuracy intervals overlap
assert overlap


The paired intervals are narrower than the intervals of the accuracies in the table above: their half-width is 2.0 to 2.7 points for the prompts with examples. That is why a lead of a few points can be clear here when the two accuracy intervals overlap.






NoteUnder the hood: why pair, and why resample pages



Two prompts scored on the same turns tend to get the same turns right: the easy ones, both; the hard ones, neither. The variance of a difference is \(\mathrm{Var}(A) + \mathrm{Var}(B) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(A, B)\), so this shared difficulty (a positive covariance) cancels in the paired difference. It is narrower than the intervals of the two accuracies once the correlation exceeds one half (for equally noisy estimates), and narrower than a comparison of independent estimates for any positive correlation.
The usual paired test, a paired \(t\)-test (scipy.stats.ttest_rel), takes this into account, but it treats every turn as an independent item. Turns of one conversation share a page, the same examples and each other’s answers, and several conversations are written from one page and share its table, so the turns are not independent, and the test’s interval is too narrow. The bootstrap here resamples whole pages, with all the conversations written from them, which keeps all of these correlations. For the two closest prompts of the table above:


Code
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.baseline_report import turn_level_paired

per_turn = turn_level_paired(scores["e3p"], scores["e3d"])
per_page = diff("e3p", "e3d")
half_page = (per_page["high"] - per_page["low"]) / 2

# ignoring the pages makes the interval too narrow, and here
# changes what it says about zero
assert per_turn["half_width"] < half_page
assert per_turn["excludes_zero"] and not per_page["excludes_zero"]


Treating turns as independent gives an interval of ±1.6 points for the lead of e3p over e3d (+0.3 to +3.5), which excludes zero. Resampling pages gives ±2.0 (-0.1 to +3.9), which does not. The selection rule uses the second.



11.6.1 What the variants show
Three things in the table are worth a closer look, and each is checked against the data before the sentence that states it is allowed to print.


Code
#HEAVY
zero_shot = diff("e0d", "e0p")
two = diff("e2d", "e2p")
three = diff("e3d", "e3p")
third_example = diff("e3p", "e2p")

# no examples, one line: it fails
assert rows["e0p"]["accuracy"] < 0.05

assert zero_shot["excludes_zero"] and zero_shot["difference"] > 0

# with examples the description does not help
assert two["difference"] <= 0 and three["difference"] <= 0
assert third_example["excludes_zero"] and third_example["difference"] > 0


The asserts in that cell hold, so the three findings can be stated:

Without examples, the one-line message fails almost completely (0.3% correct): Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 answers in prose or wraps its answer in a code block. The description changes that, to 24.0%, because it states what an answer looks like.
With examples, the description no longer helps: with two examples it is -1.3 points against the plain message, and with three -1.9. The examples already show the format, so the description has nothing to add. A third example is worth +4.4 points over the second.
Nested calls are the largest group of invalid outputs once there are examples. The DSL writes a calculation as flat steps, subtract(5, 3), divide(#0, 3), and a model that has seen other programming languages often writes it as one expression, divide(subtract(5, 3), 3), which does not run. The cell below prints three such outputs.



Code
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.baseline_report import has_nested_call

example_variants = [v for v in VARIANTS if not v.startswith("e0")]

# most invalid outputs nest
assert all(rows[v]["nested_share"] > 0.5 for v in example_variants)

# and the description makes it worse
assert rows["e3d"]["nested_share"] > rows["e3p"]["nested_share"]

invalid = {
    (s["id"], s["turn"])
    for s in scores["e3p"]
    if s["kind"] not in {
        "correct", "wrong_operations", "wrong_numbers", "wrong_answer"
    }
}

shown = sorted(
    (
        r for r in predictions["e3p"]
        if (r["id"], r["turn"]) in invalid
        and has_nested_call(r["output"])
    ),
    key=lambda r: (r["id"], r["turn"]),
)[:3]
print("\n".join(r["output"] for r in shown))


divide(subtract(0.29, 0.25), 0.25), multiply(#0, 100)
divide(subtract(331.43, 100.00), 100.00), multiply(#0, 100)
divide(subtract(1651, 1127), 1651)


With examples, more than half of the invalid outputs of every prompt nest (53.3% for the chosen one), and the description raises that share (74.0% with three examples). The description tells the model that an argument is a number, a result #k or a constant, and it reads that as a grammar in which an argument can be an expression.


11.6.2 Telling the model not to nest
That pattern suggested the obvious fix: instruct the model not to nest in the prompt. The post-hoc variant e3f adds the no-nesting rule (shown with the system messages earlier) to the description. It is the same as e3d in every other respect, so the comparison with it isolates the rule.


Code
#HEAVY
flat_vs_d, flat_vs_p = diff("e3f", "e3d"), diff("e3f", "e3p")

# the rule recovers part of the description's cost
assert flat_vs_d["difference"] > 0

# but not clearly more than the plain prompt had
assert not flat_vs_p["excludes_zero"]

# and it does not stop the nesting
assert rows["e3f"]["nested"] > 0.9 * rows["e3d"]["nested"]

assert rows["e3f"]["nested_share"] > 0.5


The rule helps a little: e3f is +1.5 points over e3d (+0.2 to +2.9), as syntax errors and bad numbers fall. But it does not stop the nesting: e3f has 138 invalid outputs that nest, against 142 for e3d, so nested calls are now 82% of what is left. And it is not clearly better than the plain prompt (0.4 points below it, with an interval that includes zero).
An instruction in the prompt is a request, and with several programs in front of it the model follows what it has seen more than what it was told. This is a point about what a prompt can do, and it matters for the question that comes back when the fine-tuned model is compared with this baseline: how much of the distance to a fine-tuned model can be crossed with a better prompt.






Brown, Tom B. et al. 2020. “Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33.


Chen, Zhiyu, Shiyang Li, Charese Smiley, Zhiqiang Ma, Sameena Shah, and William Yang Wang. 2022. “ConvFinQA: Exploring the Chain of Numerical Reasoning in Conversational Finance Question Answering.” Proceedings of EMNLP.

title: 12  Training with LoRA
text:
12.1 The data
You will learn:
Chapter 8 showed what one training step does, and Chapter 9 what a LoRA adapter is. This chapter puts the two to work: it trains an adapter for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on the training conversations, formatted as in Chapter 10. The machinery has nothing new in it. The work is in choosing the settings, and in checking while the run goes that it does what we think it does.
The run trains on train-fit, and the validation split is what it is checked against.
Code
#HEAVY
import json
import math
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from convfinqa.artifacts import artifact, get

n_fit = sum(1 for _ in get("train_val_split").jsonl("train_fit.jsonl"))
n_val = sum(1 for _ in get("train_val_split").jsonl("val.jsonl"))

print(f"Number of training conversations: {n_fit}")
print(f"Number of validation conversations: {n_val}")


Number of training conversations: 2731
Number of validation conversations: 306
There are 2,731 training conversations and 306 validation conversations. Every conversation is one training example: the system message, then the questions and answers in turn, with the loss counted on the answers only (Chapter 8, “Which tokens count”). The development split is not used here, not even to choose a checkpoint. Everything that is decided in this chapter is decided on the validation split.

title: 12  Training with LoRA
text:
12.2 The configuration settings
The settings of every run are in one file, configs/train.json: the ones all runs share, and a few entries for each named run. A light artifact, train_config_{run}, merges the two for one run, so a run’s settings are a file that can be read, and a change to one run’s entry does not change what the others were built from.


Code
@artifact("train_config_{run}", files=["configs/train.json"])
def build_train_config(out, deps, files, *, run: str):
    """Combine the base train config with the run-specific settings.

    The combined config is written to the output directory as "config.json".
    
    Args:
        out: The output directory for the combined config.
        deps: Dependencies (unused here).
        files: Dictionary of input files, keyed by their paths.
            Here the only key used is "configs/train.json".
        run: The name of the run to get the specific settings for.
    """
    import json

    from convfinqa.train_config import run_config

    cfg = run_config(files["configs/train.json"].json(), run)
    (out / "config.json").write_text(json.dumps(cfg, indent=2))


The settings of the main run that decide how it behaves (the smoke run of the next section differs in three of them):


Code
#HEAVY
cfg = get("train_config_main").json("config.json")
smoke = get("train_config_smoke").json("config.json")

# Strip leading zero in scientific notation exponent
sci = lambda x: f"{x:.0e}".replace("e-0", "e-")

# Get the demo run results from 205_how_fine_tuning.qmd
# and extract the learning rate history.
demo = get("sft_demo").json("result.json")
full_lr = max(
    h["learning_rate"]
    for h in demo["log_history"]
    if "learning_rate" in h

# Extract config settings and output as a dataframe

steps_per_epoch = math.ceil(
    n_fit / (cfg["micro_batch"] * cfg["accumulation"])
)
steps = steps_per_epoch * cfg["epochs"]
warmup = math.ceil(cfg["warmup_ratio"] * steps)

micro-batch × accumulation
4 × 4


epochs
2


optimizer steps
342 (171 per epoch)


maximum length (tokens)
3,584


evaluation on validation every
50 steps


gradient checkpointing
on







Most of these were explained in the chapters before this one. The reasons, in order:
LoRA. Rank 16, alpha 32 (so the update is scaled by \(\alpha / r =\) 2), dropout 0.05 on the adapter’s input, and an adapter on every linear layer of the decoder (all-linear): the seven matrices of Chapter 9. The model’s own weights stay in bf16 and the adapter, which is what trains, in fp32. The rank is a guess at how much freedom the task needs, and Chapter 17 returns to it.
The learning rate and its schedule. A peak of 2e-4, reached after a linear warmup of 11 steps and then falling along half a cosine wave to zero by step 342 (Chapter 8, “The learning-rate schedule”). The rate is 10 times that of the full fine-tuning run of Chapter 8 (2e-5): the adapter starts at zero and has to travel to be useful, and it has far fewer weights to move.
The batch. Micro-batches of 4 conversations, with 4 of them accumulated into each update, so each update uses 16 conversations. With 2,731 conversations that makes 171 steps an epoch, and 342 in the 2 epochs. Gradient clipping at a norm of 1.0 guards against one odd batch.
Weight decay. It is zero. Weight decay pulls every trainable weight a little towards zero at each step, a brake on weights that would otherwise keep growing. It earns its keep when a large network trains for a long time on much data. Here the adapter starts at zero, trains for about 342 steps, and the checkpoint is chosen by its validation loss, which already guards against training for too long. Pulling the adapter towards zero would also pull the model towards where it started, which the learning rate and the choice of checkpoint control more directly. If the validation loss turns up while the training loss still falls, this is the first setting to revisit.
Length and memory. Conversations are cut at 3,584 tokens (the longest in the data is 3,460, Chapter 2, so nothing is cut). Gradient checkpointing is on, as in Chapter 8, because the activations of such long sequences would otherwise take more memory than the weights do. The process is capped at 80 GB of the GPU’s memory, which the desktop shares.

title: 12  Training with LoRA
text:
12.3 The two runs


Code
# the smoke run changes the model and the length of the run,
# and nothing about how the model learns
assert {k for k in cfg if cfg[k] != smoke[k]} \
    == {"model", "max_steps", "eval_every"}
assert cfg["weight_decay"] == 0


The smoke run trains Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct for 50 steps with the same recipe. It takes minutes, and is there to check the whole chain (the data, the training, the choice of the best checkpoint, the numbers recorded) before the main run spends hours. Nothing is concluded from its accuracy, and the book does not build it by default: python -m convfinqa.artifacts build check_lora_smoke_0 runs it. It changes only the model, the number of steps and how often the validation loss is measured. The main run trains Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 for the full 342 steps.
Both runs measure the loss on the validation conversations before the first step and then every 50 steps (every 10 for the smoke run), and at the end. Only the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is kept, as the adapter that the rest of the book uses.
The validation loss is the mean over answer tokens, so that every answer token weighs the same, as in the training loss and in the loss of the untuned model measured in Chapter 7. (The Trainer’s own evaluation averages the mean losses of the conversations instead, which gives a short conversation the weight of a long one; the training code corrects for that, so that the first validation loss can be compared with the untuned model’s.)
Two artifacts carry a run, both named by the run (smoke, main) and the seed of the training. lora_{run}_{seed} trains the adapter and writes it with the loss history. check_lora_{run}_{seed} loads the adapter and measures its accuracy on a small sample of validation turns. The training itself is convfinqa.finetune.train_lora: the chapter holds the settings and the calls, the package the logic.


Code
@artifact(
    "lora_{run}_{seed}",
    deps=["train_val_split", "train_config_{run}"],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_lora(out, deps, *, run: str, seed: int):
    """
    Build and train the LoRA adapter for a given run and seed.

    Args:
        out : The output directory for the adapter and training state.
        deps : The dependencies, including the training configuration
            and data splits.
        run : The run identifier, e.g., "smoke" or "main".
        seed : The random seed for training.
    """
    import json

    from convfinqa.finetune import train_lora

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    fit = list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("train_fit.jsonl"))
    val = list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl"))
    result = train_lora(cfg, fit, val, out, seed)
    history = {k: result.pop(k) for k in ("log_history", "max_steps")}
    (out / "trainer_state.json").write_text(json.dumps(history))
    (out / "metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


@artifact(
    "check_lora_{run}_{seed}",
    deps=[
        "lora_{run}_{seed}", "train_config_{run}",
        "train_val_split", "eval_turns",
    ],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_check_lora(out, deps, *, run: str, seed: int):
    """
    Evaluate the LoRA adapter trained by `build_lora`.

    Does not call `build_lora` itself; the results are loaded
    from the dependencies.

    Args:
        out : The output directory for the check results.
        deps : The dependencies, including the adapter, training
            configuration, and data splits.
        run : The run identifier, e.g., "smoke" or "main".
        seed : The random seed for training.
    """
    import json

    from convfinqa.finetune import check_adapter

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    result = check_adapter(
        cfg,
        deps[f"lora_{run}_{seed}"].path / "adapter",
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("val_turns.jsonl")),
    )
    (out / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(result["summary"], indent=2))
    (out / "scores.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(s) + "\n" for s in result["scores"])
    )
    (out / "predictions.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(p) + "\n" for p in result["predictions"])
    )

Figure 12.1: Loss over the main run. The dots are the training loss of each optimizer step; the squares are the validation loss at step 0 and every 50 steps. The ring marks the checkpoint that is kept, the one with the lowest validation loss.





The validation loss starts at 2.2062, which is the untuned model’s loss of Chapter 7, now measured through the training code, so the two agree. By step 50 it has fallen to 0.052, 42-fold. It keeps falling at every check up to step 250, where it reaches 0.0357. The first check alone covers over 90% of the whole fall. The last two checks are within 0.3% of it: the loss has levelled off while the learning rate falls along the tail of the cosine (Figure 8.3). The kept adapter is the one from step 250, of the 342 steps the run took. The loss is not rising again, so the run shows no sign of overfitting, and the weight decay of zero was not a problem.


Code

assert train_tail < best


The training loss over the last 50 steps averages 0.018, below the validation loss 0.036 of the kept checkpoint, as expected: the adapter has seen those conversations and not these. The training loss is a mean over single batches and is noisy, so the two are compared only roughly.

title: 12  Training with LoRA
text:
12.6 What the adapter changed
The adapter is a set of pairs \((A, B)\), and each pair stands for an update \(\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r} B A\) to one weight matrix. We can look at the updates themselves. The first artifact reads the saved adapter and, for every one of the adapted matrices, the size of the update (its Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of its squared entries) relative to the size of the weight matrix it modifies, and the singular values of the update (explained below).


Code
#HEAVY
# Generate the adapter-to-base-weight analysis
# For each layer and matrix kind, compute the ratio of the update's norm
# to the base weight's norm. Also compute the share of the update's squared norm
# captured by each singular value.
@artifact(
    "adapter_analysis_{run}_{seed}",
    deps=["lora_{run}_{seed}", "train_config_{run}"],
)
def build_adapter_analysis(out, deps, *, run: str, seed: int):
    import json

    from convfinqa.adapter_stats import adapter_update_stats, base_weight_norms

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    stats = adapter_update_stats(deps[f"lora_{run}_{seed}"].path / "adapter")
    base = base_weight_norms(cfg["model"])
    for m in stats["matrices"]:
        m["relative_norm"] = m["norm"] / base[(m["layer"], m["module"])]
    (out / "stats.json").write_text(json.dumps(stats))


stats = get("adapter_analysis_main_0").json("stats.json")
mods, n_layers = stats["modules"], stats["layers"]
relative = np.zeros((n_layers, len(mods)))
for m in stats["matrices"]:
    relative[m["layer"], mods.index(m["module"])] = m["relative_norm"]
sq_sv = np.array([m["singular_values"] for m in stats["matrices"]]) ** 2
sq_share = sq_sv / sq_sv.sum(1, keepdims=True)
cumulative = sq_share.cumsum(1).mean(0)
K = 7

# the update is small next to the weight, and does not sit on one direction
assert relative.max() < 0.02
assert sq_share[:, 0].mean() < 0.75 and cumulative[7] > 0.85




Code
# Plot a heatmap of the update norm ratios by layer and matrix kind
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5))
im = ax.imshow(100 * relative, aspect="auto", cmap="viridis")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(mods)), [m.replace("_proj", "") for m in mods])
ax.set_ylabel("layer")
ax.set_xlabel("matrix")
fig.colorbar(im, label="‖ΔW‖ / ‖W‖ (%)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 12.2: The size of the adapter’s update to each adapted matrix, as a percentage of the norm of the matrix, by layer (rows) and kind of matrix (columns).





The updates are small: the largest is 1.3% of the norm of its weight matrix, and the average over all 252 matrices 0.80%. The model has been changed by a small amount in many places, not by a lot in a few: by kind of matrix the averages run from 0.54% (down_proj) to 0.93% (gate_proj).
The following figure shows how the squared norm of the update is distributed across its singular values, indicating the effective rank of the update.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(range(1, len(cumulative) + 1), cumulative, "o-", ms=4)
ax.set_xlabel("number of singular values, k")
ax.set_ylabel("share of squared norm")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 12.3: How the squared norm of the update is spread over its directions: the share held by the largest k singular values, averaged over the adapted matrices.





The rank \(r =\) 16 is used: the largest singular value holds on average 56% of an update’s squared norm, and it takes 7 of the 16 directions to hold 90%.






NoteUnder the hood: what the singular values say



A matrix of rank 16 is a sum of 16 rank-1 matrices. A rank-1 matrix is a column times a row, \(\sigma\, u v^\top\): it reads the input along one direction (the row \(v^\top\)), scales it by \(\sigma\), and writes the result along one direction of the output (the column \(u\)). This is the usual form \(U \Sigma V^\top\) of the singular value decomposition written out column by column: \(\Delta W = \sum_i \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top\), with \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots\) the singular values and the \(u_i\) (and the \(v_i\)) perpendicular to each other. The squared size of the matrix (the squared Frobenius norm) is the sum of the squared singular values, which is why the figure shows squared norms: each singular value takes its share.
Keeping only the \(k\) largest terms of the sum gives a matrix of rank \(k\), and it is the closest matrix of rank \(k\) to the original: no other comes nearer (the Eckart–Young theorem). The squared distance is the squared singular values that were dropped. So the curve of Figure 12.3 can be read the other way round: the best stand-in of rank 7 for an update of rank 16 would be off by 9% of the update’s squared norm, on average over the matrices.
Two cautions. The stand-in is closest in the weights, not necessarily in what the model does: a small term can still matter. And it is not what an adapter of rank 7 trained from scratch would find, because that one is fitted to the task, not cut from this one. The rank sweep later in the book tests that directly.








NoteFurther reading



These sizes are the sizes of the update, not of its effect: a small change in the right place can change the output a lot, and a large one in a direction the data never uses changes nothing. The next section looks at the effect directly, on the tokens themselves. Hu et al. (2022) found that a very small rank was often enough for the update of a language model, which is the other side of the same question.

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.1 Two histories
You will learn:
Chapter 12 ended with a quick check: a sample of turns, with the gold history, to see that the adapter that was saved is the one that learned. This chapter is the evaluation itself: every turn of the split, with the history the model would have in use, scored the way the untuned baseline of Chapter 11 was scored, so that the two can be compared.
Everything here is measured on the validation split, which is where the book makes its choices. The development split is used once, at the end, for the final numbers of the fine-tuned model and of the untuned baselines it is compared with (the two histories, with the code of this chapter and nothing else): the evaluations are artifacts named by the split, and the final chapter asks for the same ones with dev. The other comparisons of this chapter (the examples on the tuned model, the extra compute, the merged adapter) are validation results only.
A conversation is a sequence of questions, and each answer can use the earlier ones: “and what is that as a percentage?” is a question about the answer before it. When the model answers turn \(k\), the prompt holds the turns before it, and there are two ways to fill in the model’s side of them.
Gold-history accuracy is what predicted-history accuracy would be if no earlier mistake carried over, and the gap between the two, turn by turn, shows how far errors compound. No conversation and no turn is dropped in either mode: a turn that follows a wrong answer is still scored.

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
Gold history. The earlier answers are the gold programs, as in training. This is called teacher forcing: the model is never shown its own mistakes. Each turn is an independent question with the right context, so the score says how well the model answers when everything before it was right.
Predicted history. The earlier answers are the model’s own outputs, exactly as generated, valid or not. This is how the model would be used: a mistake at turn 2 is in the prompt at turn 3. It is the headline mode of the book.

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.2 The policy for invalid outputs
Decoding is greedy, with one attempt per turn, and an output that is not a valid program, or that does not execute, counts as wrong. The denominator is every turn. This is what the official ConvFinQA evaluation does, and what the published numbers we compare with assume. In predicted history, an invalid output stays in the history as it was generated. The share of invalid outputs is reported next to the accuracy, by cause, because it says where the errors are: not being able to write the language, or writing it wrongly.

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.3 The code
Two artifacts evaluate a run. Both are named by the split, the run, the seed of the training and the history mode. tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode} loads the adapter of Chapter 12 and writes one output per turn, with the training prompt and no examples; like the baseline’s, it refuses dev until the freeze file exists. scores_tuned_… is light: it executes and scores the outputs. The generation is convfinqa.tuned_eval.generate_tuned.


Code
from convfinqa.artifacts import artifact, get


@artifact(
    "tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=[
        "train_val_split", "eval_turns",
        "lora_{run}_{seed}", "train_config_{run}",
    ],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_tuned(out, deps, *, split: str, run: str, seed: int, mode: str):
    """Generate the fine-tuned model's output for every turn of a split.

    Args:
        out: Output directory; `predictions.jsonl` is written to it.
        deps: The adapter, its settings and the conversations.
        split: `val`, or `dev` once `configs/FROZEN` exists.
        run: The training run (`main`).
        seed: The seed of the training.
        mode: `gold` or `pred`, the history of the earlier turns.
    """
    import json
    import time

    from convfinqa.tuned_eval import generate_tuned, split_conversations

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    convs = split_conversations(
        split,
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl")),
    )
    start, done = time.perf_counter(), 0
    with open(out / "predictions.jsonl", "w") as f:
        def sink(row):
            nonlocal done
            f.write(json.dumps({
                k: v for k, v in row.items() if k != "seconds"
            }) + "\n")   # timing is not an output
            f.flush()
            done += 1
            if done % 50 == 0:
                print(
                    f"{done} turns, {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s",
                    flush=True
                )

        generate_tuned(
            cfg, deps[f"lora_{run}_{seed}"].path / "adapter",
            convs, mode, sink
        )
    print(f"done: {done} turns in {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s")


@artifact(
    "scores_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=["tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}", "eval_turns"],
)
def build_scores_tuned(out, deps, *, split: str, run: str, seed: int, mode: str):
    """Execute and score the outputs of `tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}`."""
    import json

    from convfinqa.evaluate import score_rows, summarize
    from convfinqa.program_match import add_program_match

    rows = list(
        deps[f"tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}"].jsonl("predictions.jsonl")
    )
    turns = list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl"))
    scores = add_program_match(score_rows(rows, turns), rows, turns)
    (out / "scores.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(s) + "\n" for s in scores)
    )
    (out / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(summarize(scores), indent=2)
    )

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.4 Results on the validation split
The fine-tuned model uses the adapter that Chapter 12 kept (the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss, seed 0). We run this model using the same prompt as in training: the one-line system message and no examples, denoted e0p in Chapter 11. This is compared against the untuned model using both e0p and e3p, which adds three examples to the system prompt: the former shows what fine-tuning changed, while the latter shows what is left for fine-tuning to add after the prompt has done its best. All the systems are scored on the same validation turns, so differences between them are measured paired, by resampling whole report pages (Chapter 11, “Under the hood: why pair, and why resample pages”).

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.5 Beyond execution accuracy
Execution accuracy asks only whether the number is right. Two further measures look at the program itself and at the numbers it is written with, and the error analysis below uses both.

13.5.1 Program accuracy
Execution accuracy asks whether the program gives the right number. Program accuracy asks whether it is the right program, by the rule of the official ConvFinQA script. The two programs are compared as expressions, so the operands of an add or a multiply may come in either order, and a calculation may be split over the steps in another way. The arguments are compared as exact text: the numbers must be copied off the page as they are, so 2.70 is not 2.7, and 17% is not 0.17. A program that reaches the right answer from other numbers is not the gold program either.
Because the gold program gives the gold answer, a turn that is right by program is right by execution too. The interesting counts are the other way round: how much program accuracy loses against execution accuracy, and what the turns in between look like.


Code
#HEAVY
import re

from convfinqa.program_match import equal_up_to_constants

names = {
    "zero": "untuned_val_e0p_0_pred",
    "base": "untuned_val_e3p_0_pred",
    "pred": "tuned_val_main_0_pred",
    "gold": "tuned_val_main_0_gold",
}
for key, name in names.items():
    scores[key] = list(get(f"scores_{name}").jsonl("scores.jsonl"))
program = {
    key: [{**s, "correct": s["program_correct"]} for s in rows_]
    for key, rows_ in scores.items()
}
ci_program = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in program.items()}
exact_text = {
    k: sum(s["text_match"] for s in v) / len(v)
    for k, v in scores.items()
}
swapped = {  # the same program, written in another order
    k: sum(s["program_correct"] and not s["text_match"] for s in v)
    for k, v in scores.items()
}
loses = {
    k: sum(s["correct"] and not s["program_correct"] for s in v)
    for k, v in scores.items()
}

# program-correct implies execution-correct
assert not any(
    s["program_correct"] and not s["correct"]
    for v in scores.values()
    for s in v
)

pd.DataFrame({
    label: {
        "execution accuracy": f"{ci[k]['accuracy']:.1%}",
        "program accuracy": f"{ci_program[k]['accuracy']:.1%}",
        "95% interval":
            f"[{ci_program[k]['low']:.1%}, {ci_program[k]['high']:.1%}]",
        "same text as gold": f"{exact_text[k]:.1%}",
        "right answer, other program": loses[k],
    }
    for label, k in (
        ("untuned, e0p", "zero"),
        ("untuned, e3p", "base"),
        ("fine-tuned, predicted", "pred"),
        ("fine-tuned, gold", "gold"),

13.5.1.2 Other programs with the right answer
What does the fine-tuned model lose against its execution accuracy? The turns that have the right answer and another program, grouped by how the program differs from the gold one:


Code
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.mistake_kinds import KINDS, minimal_explanations

other = [s for s in scores["pred"] if s["correct"] and not s["program_correct"]]
GROUPS = {
    ("constants",): "a constant written as a number",
    ("constants", "zeros"): "that, with trailing zeros",
    ("signs",): "signs dropped, cancelling in a ratio",
}

def group_of(s):
    key = (s["id"], s["turn"])
    found = minimal_explanations(output_of[key], gold_of[key])
    return tuple(k for k in KINDS if found and k in found[0]) if found else None

members = {}
for s in other:
    members.setdefault(GROUPS.get(group_of(s), "other"), []).append(s)
sizes = [len(v) for k, v in members.items() if k != "other"]

# the spelling of a constant is the largest group
assert max(members, key=lambda k: len(members[k])) == "a constant written as a number"

# execution accuracy is much closer to program accuracy for the
# fine-tuned model than for the untuned one
assert loses["pred"] < loses["base"] / 2

# the three named groups hold most of these turns
assert sum(sizes) > 3 / 4 * len(other)

    }
    for label, v in sorted(
        members.items(),
        key=lambda kv: (kv[0] == "other", -len(kv[1]))
    )
]).set_index("difference from the gold program")

23 turns have the right answer with another program. The largest group is the spelling of a constant: the gold programs write the number 100 as const_100 in some conversations and as 100 in others, and the model chooses one of them. The official rule counts that as a different program, and so do we, but it says little about the model. The gold also writes a loss as a negative number, and where the model drops the sign the answer survives only if the signs cancel, as in a ratio of two losses. The other 5 turns differ in other ways. For the untuned model with e3p, many more turns have the right answer with another program (84).



13.5.2 Where the numbers come from
Program accuracy compares whole programs. The literal check looks only at the numbers a program is written with, and so it works for any output format. For each turn it asks three things: are the numbers the same as the gold program’s as text, are they the same as values (2.70 is 2.7, 17% is 0.17, const_100 is 100), and is every number that is not a named constant from the page, as text. The gap between the first two is formatting; the third says whether the numbers were copied, not made up. The scale check is separate: it asks whether the answer is the gold answer times a power of ten.


Code
@artifact(
    "checks_untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=[
        "untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}",
        "eval_turns", "train_val_split",
    ],
)
def build_checks_untuned(
    out, deps, *, split: str, variant: str, seed: int, mode: str
):
    """The literal and scale checks of an untuned run."""
    import json

    from convfinqa.output_checks import check_rows
    from convfinqa.tuned_eval import split_conversations

    convs = split_conversations(
        split,
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl")),
    )
    rows = list(
        deps[f"untuned_{split}_{variant}_{seed}_{mode}"]
        .jsonl("predictions.jsonl")
    )
    checks = check_rows(
        rows, list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl")), convs
    )
    (out / "checks.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(c) + "\n" for c in checks)
    )


@artifact(
    "checks_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}",
    deps=[
        "tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}", "eval_turns", "train_val_split",
    ],
)
def build_checks_tuned(out, deps, *, split: str, run: str, seed: int, mode: str):
    """The literal and scale checks of a fine-tuned run."""
    import json

    from convfinqa.output_checks import check_rows
    from convfinqa.tuned_eval import split_conversations

    convs = split_conversations(
        split,
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl")),
    )
    rows = list(
        deps[f"tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{mode}"].jsonl("predictions.jsonl")
    )
    checks = check_rows(
        rows, list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl")), convs
    )
    (out / "checks.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(c) + "\n" for c in checks)
    )

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.6 Error analysis
This section asks what the fine-tuned model gets wrong: first by the kind of outcome, then by the likely cause, and then by how close the model was to the right token at the point where it went wrong.

13.6.1 Where the failures are


Code
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.evaluate import RUNS
from convfinqa.final_results import outcome_counts

outcomes = pd.DataFrame({
    "untuned, e0p": outcome_counts(summary["zero"]),
    "untuned, e3p": outcome_counts(summary["base"]),
    "fine-tuned, predicted": outcome_counts(summary["pred"]),
    "fine-tuned, gold": outcome_counts(summary["gold"]),
})
invalid = {key: outcome_counts(summary[key])["invalid output"] for key in summary}
wrong = {
    key: summary[key]["n"] - summary[key]["by_kind"]["correct"]
    for key in summary
}
causes = {k: v for k, v in summary["zero"]["by_kind"].items() if k not in RUNS}
fence = causes["code_fence"]

# what is left after fine-tuning is almost all valid programs that are wrong
assert invalid["pred"] <= 0.05 * wrong["pred"]
assert invalid["pred"] < invalid["base"]
# most of the untuned model's invalid outputs are a program in a code fence
assert fence == max(causes.values()) and fence > invalid["zero"] / 2
# the most common failure of the fine-tuned model is other numbers
assert outcomes.loc["wrong numbers", "fine-tuned, predicted"]\
    == outcomes.loc[
        ["wrong operations", "wrong numbers", "wrong answer, right shape"],
        "fine-tuned, predicted"
    ].max()

After fine-tuning it is 0 of 183 (0 with the gold history). What is left is a valid program that is wrong: a different operation, different numbers, or the right shape with the wrong value. Different numbers are the largest of the three, 74 of the 183 wrong turns. That is a failure of reading the page and reasoning, and not of writing the language.


13.6.2 What the fine-tuned model gets wrong
The turns the fine-tuned model gets wrong are valid programs, so the question is why they are wrong. Each wrong turn of the predicted-history run gets one label, the first of these that applies: it is not a program that runs; it is right when the earlier answers are the gold ones, so the history is the likely cause; the answer is off by a power of ten; it is the negative of the gold answer, because a sign was dropped or the operands of a subtraction were reversed; a number is not from the page; the program has the same operations as the gold with other numbers (or another number was copied where a number was asked for); it has other operations; or none of these.

#HEAVY

from convfinqa.mistake_kinds import count_minimal_sets

The program differs from the gold in 206 of the 1125 turns. Four kinds of difference are about the form and not the content: a constant written as a number, trailing zeros, signs, and the order of the operands of a subtraction or a division. They explain 46 of the 206, alone or together, and no turn has two alternative explanations. The other 160 differ in what the program says.


13.6.3 How close was the right token?
A wrong program is a sequence of token choices. The gold program and the model’s are the same text up to the first token where they differ, so up to there the model chose as the gold program does, and its distribution at that position is the one it wrote its own token from. Its rank for the gold token there (1 is the most probable token), and the ratio of the gold token’s probability to the probability of the token it wrote, say whether the right answer was a near miss or far away. divergence_{split}_{run}_{seed} scores the wrong turns of the predicted-history run with the same prompts, in one forward pass each.


Code
@artifact(
    "divergence_{split}_{run}_{seed}",
    deps=[
        "train_val_split", "eval_turns",
        "lora_{run}_{seed}", "train_config_{run}",
        "tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_pred",
        "scores_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_pred",
    ],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_divergence(out, deps, *, split: str, run: str, seed: int):
    """Score the first token where each wrong program differs from the gold one.

    Args:
        out: Output directory; `divergences.jsonl` is written to it.
        deps: The adapter, the conversations and the predicted-history run.
        split: `val`, or `dev` once `configs/FROZEN` exists.
        run: The training run (`main`).
        seed: The seed of the training.
    """
    import json

    from convfinqa.divergence import score_divergences
    from convfinqa.tuned_eval import split_conversations

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    convs = split_conversations(
        split,
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl")),
    )
    rows = list(
        deps[f"tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_pred"].jsonl("predictions.jsonl")
    )
    turns = list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl"))
    scores = deps[f"scores_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_pred"].jsonl(
        "scores.jsonl"
    )
    wrong = {(s["id"], s["turn"]) for s in scores if not s["correct"]}
    results = score_divergences(
        cfg, deps[f"lora_{run}_{seed}"].path / "adapter",
        convs, rows, turns, wrong
    )
    (out / "divergences.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in results)
    )

At the first token where the two programs differ, the gold token is among the model’s top three in 89% of the 183 wrong turns, and in the second place in 128 of them. The model’s own token was the most probable one in 100% of the turns, so the re-scoring reproduces what it wrote. The gold token ranks first in 0 turns, where it shares the first place with the model’s token in an exact tie. The gap in probability is usually larger than the gap in rank suggests: the median ratio of the gold token’s probability to the model’s is 0.013, and the gold token comes within a factor of ten in 27% of the turns. The model is rarely lost; at the point where it goes wrong it had the right token near the top, but gave the token it wrote a median probability of 98%. By type of mistake, the dropped signs are the near misses (the gold token is within a factor of ten in 70% of those turns), while in the turns that are wrong only because of the earlier answers it is within a factor of ten in 11%: with its own history in the prompt, the model was sure of the program it wrote.

title: 13  Evaluating the fine-tuned model
text:
13.7 Variations on the setup

13.7.1 Does a prompt still help the tuned model?
The adapter was trained on the one-line prompt and no examples. Fine-tuning and prompting are two routes to the same end, and nothing says that they cannot be taken together: the same three examples that did the most for the untuned model (e3p) can be put in front of the tuned one. If they help, the two routes add up. If they do not, the adapter has already taken up what the examples were teaching, or the examples are now an input unlike any that it was trained on, and get in the way.
prompted_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{variant}_{shots}_{mode} asks the tuned model with a prompt variant of Chapter 11: variant names the variant and shots the example set, as in the baseline’s artifacts. The examples come from the training conversations, as they did there.


Code
@artifact(
    "prompted_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{variant}_{shots}_{mode}",
    deps=[
        "train_val_split", "eval_turns", "example_sets",
        "lora_{run}_{seed}", "train_config_{run}",
    ],
    files=["configs/baseline.json"],
    heavy=True,
)
def build_prompted_tuned(
    out, deps, files, *,
    split: str, run: str, seed: int, variant: str, shots: int, mode: str
):
    """Generate the fine-tuned model's output with a baseline prompt.

    Args:
        out: Output directory; `predictions.jsonl` is written to it.
        deps: The adapter, its settings, the conversations and the example sets.
        files: `configs/baseline.json`, which holds the system messages.
        split: `val`, or `dev` once `configs/FROZEN` exists.
        run: The training run (`main`).
        seed: The seed of the training.
        variant: The prompt variant of the baseline (`e3p`).
        shots: The example set.
        mode: `gold` or `pred`, the history of the earlier turns.
    """
    import json
    import time

    from convfinqa.tuned_eval import split_conversations
    from convfinqa.tuned_prompted import (
        baseline_prompt, generate_tuned_prompted
    )

    cfg = deps[f"train_config_{run}"].json("config.json")
    convs = split_conversations(
        split,
        list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")),
        list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl("dev.jsonl")),
    )
    pool = {
        c["id"]: c for c in deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("train_fit.jsonl")
    }
    system, examples = baseline_prompt(
        files["configs/baseline.json"].json(),
        deps["example_sets"].json("sets.json"), pool, variant, shots
    )
    start, done = time.perf_counter(), 0
    with open(out / "predictions.jsonl", "w") as f:
        def sink(row):
            nonlocal done
            f.write(json.dumps({
                k: v for k, v in row.items() if k != "seconds"
            }) + "\n")   # timing is not an output
            f.flush()
            done += 1
            if done % 50 == 0:
                print(
                    f"{done} turns, {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s",
                    flush=True
                )

        generate_tuned_prompted(
            cfg, deps[f"lora_{run}_{seed}"].path / "adapter",
            convs, system, examples, mode, sink
        )
    print(f"done: {done} turns in {time.perf_counter() - start:.0f} s")


@artifact(
    "scores_prompted_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{variant}_{shots}_{mode}",
    deps=[
        "prompted_tuned_{split}_{run}_{seed}_{variant}_{shots}_{mode}",
        "eval_turns",
    ],
)
def build_scores_prompted_tuned(
    out, deps, *,
    split: str, run: str, seed: int, variant: str, shots: int, mode: str
):
    """Execute and score the outputs of `prompted_tuned_…`."""
    import json

    from convfinqa.evaluate import score_rows, summarize
    from convfinqa.program_match import add_program_match

    name = f"{split}_{run}_{seed}_{variant}_{shots}_{mode}"
    rows = list(deps[f"prompted_tuned_{name}"].jsonl("predictions.jsonl"))
    turns = list(deps["eval_turns"].jsonl(f"{split}_turns.jsonl"))
    scores = add_program_match(score_rows(rows, turns), rows, turns)
    (out / "scores.jsonl").write_text(
        "".join(json.dumps(s) + "\n" for s in scores)
    )
    (out / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(summarize(scores), indent=2)
    )
