title: 17  How much rank does the task need?
text:
17.7 Other things one could try
The sweep is the one new experiment of this chapter. The other ideas that came up while writing the book are not run, for one of two reasons: the results we already have say that they would not help, or they cost more than the project can show a gain for. The first kind is checked below against the validation results; the second is described, with the reason.

17.7.1 Not needed: what the results already say


Code
#HEAVY
import json

from convfinqa.stats import bootstrap_accuracy, paired_difference

main_pred = get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_pred")
main_scores = list(main_pred.jsonl("scores.jsonl"))
main_sum = main_pred.json("summary.json")
n_val = main_sum["n"]
n_invalid = round(main_sum["invalid_rate"] * n_val)
n_bad_reference = main_sum["by_kind"].get("bad_reference", 0)

# DSL adapter: the numbers it writes, checked against the page (@sec-evaluating-errors)
dsl_checks = [
    c for c in get("checks_tuned_val_main_0_pred").jsonl("checks.jsonl")
    if c["runs"]
]
dsl_off_page = sum(not c["lit_grounded"] for c in dsl_checks)
assert dsl_off_page == 0
# the fine-tuned model writes almost nothing invalid, and what it does is a bad reference
assert n_invalid <= 1
assert n_bad_reference == n_invalid

# Python adapter against the DSL adapter (@sec-python-numbers)
py_scores = list(
    get("scores_python_tuned_val_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl")
)
py_lead = paired_difference(py_scores, main_scores)
assert not py_lead["excludes_zero"]
pts = lambda x: f"{100 * x:+.1f}"


Three ideas would add a constraint or a variant that the results show to be unnecessary.

A grammar that allows only numbers from the page. 0 of the 1,125 programs of the adapter that run contain a number that is not on the page (Section 13.6.2), so such a grammar would have nothing to forbid. It is the untuned model that writes numbers that are not on the page (Section 14.9).
A grammar for the #k references to earlier steps. Of the 1,125 validation turns of the fine-tuned model, 0 are invalid, and 0 of them are a reference to a step that does not exist (Section 15.4). A grammar for references could fix at most those 0 turns.
A Python variant where variables persist across turns, like a notebook. The Python adapter is -0.3 points from the DSL adapter on the validation turns, with a paired interval of -2.4 to +1.7 (predicted history), so a second Python variant would be measured against a tie.

A fourth idea, more training data written by hand or generated, was planned as a chapter of its own and dropped: the chapter used no model, built one example, and could check only its form, so it did not show how such data would be used by the rest of the book.


17.7.2 Not tried, and why


Code
#HEAVY
vote = list(get("extra_val_main_0_vote_full").jsonl("predictions.jsonl"))
group = vote[0]["generations"]
unanimous = sum(v["agreement"] == 1 for v in vote) / len(vote)
half_width = bootstrap_accuracy(main_scores)
half_width = (half_width["high"] - half_width["low"]) / 2
assert unanimous > 0.8
assert half_width > 0.02



A stronger model, untuned or fine-tuned. An untuned stronger model says little about this project, which asks what fine-tuning a small model on the language of the task gains. A fine-tuned larger one is the same experiment at another size, and a project of its own, with its own cost.
Page images in place of text, with a vision-language model, and LoRA on its language layers only. The data gives each page as extracted text and a table, and the reports they come from are not part of it; we did not find where to get them. There is nothing to give such a model.
Reinforcement learning with the executor as the reward. The execution of a program already gives a reward that needs no judge: 1 if the answer matches, 0 if not. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al. 2024) samples a group of programs per prompt, scores each, and moves the model towards the ones that score above the average of their group. Liu et al. (2025) trained a 7B model this way, starting from a model that had been fine-tuned on examples, and report on ConvFinQA a score of 81.0 for the model before and 85.0 after, on their own sample of questions and prompts, so the numbers are not comparable with ours. Three things argue against running it here, and the first two can be read from the book.
First, the signal. The samples of a group that agree on the answer get the same reward, and a group with a single reward has no program that scores above the others. In the self-consistency run of Chapter 13, 5 samples per turn agreed on the answer for 91% of the validation turns. A group of eight, which is what TRL uses by default, has more room to disagree, but most of the turns would still give little. Second, the size of a gain. The accuracy of the fine-tuned model on this split has an interval of about ±3.9 points, so a gain of one or two points is small beside it. A paired comparison is tighter than that, but one seed adds a variation that is not measured (see “What is decided before the results” above). Third, the cost: each prompt needs a full-length sequence for each member of the group, generated during training. The idea is left for a project with more data, more seeds and more budget.
Training on the model’s own predicted history, which would remove the gap between training and use that Chapter 13 measures, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces, which needs a teacher model to write them. The first needs generation inside the training loop, like the reinforcement learning above, and the second needs a model that we do not have.







Liu, Zhaowei et al. 2025. “Fin-R1: A Large Language Model for Financial Reasoning Through Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.16252.


Shao, Zhihong, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, et al. 2024. “DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2402.03300.

title: 18  Summary
text:
Code
#HEAVY
from convfinqa.artifacts import get
from convfinqa.stats import bootstrap_accuracy, paired_difference

DEV = {
    ("fine-tuned", "pred"): "scores_tuned_dev_main_0_pred",
    ("fine-tuned", "gold"): "scores_tuned_dev_main_0_gold",
    ("e3p", "pred"): "scores_untuned_dev_e3p_0_pred",
    ("e0p", "pred"): "scores_untuned_dev_e0p_0_pred",
}
dev = {k: list(get(name).jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for k, name in DEV.items()}
acc = {k: bootstrap_accuracy(v) for k, v in dev.items()}
lead_e3p = paired_difference(dev[("fine-tuned", "pred")], dev[("e3p", "pred")])
lead_e0p = paired_difference(dev[("fine-tuned", "pred")], dev[("e0p", "pred")])
n_dev_turns = len(dev[("fine-tuned", "pred")])
# the fine-tuned model is ahead of both untuned systems by more than the resampling noise (@sec-final)
assert lead_e3p["excludes_zero"] and lead_e3p["difference"] > 0
assert lead_e0p["excludes_zero"] and lead_e0p["difference"] > lead_e3p["difference"]
# and the gold history is ahead of the predicted one
assert acc[("fine-tuned", "gold")]["accuracy"] > acc[("fine-tuned", "pred")]["accuracy"]

run = get("lora_main_0")
metrics = run.json("metrics.json")
max_steps = run.json("trainer_state.json")["max_steps"]
hours = metrics["train_seconds"] / 3600
# as a share of the base model, as in @sec-lora (total_params counts the adapter too)
share = metrics["trainable_params"] / (metrics["total_params"] - metrics["trainable_params"])
# the validation loss falls by a large factor, and the kept checkpoint is the lowest one (@sec-training)
assert metrics["best_eval_loss"] < metrics["step0_eval_loss"] / 10

val_main = list(get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl"))
python = paired_difference(list(get("scores_python_tuned_val_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl")), val_main)
# after fine-tuning, DSL and Python are tied (@sec-python-format)
assert not python["excludes_zero"]

untuned_free = paired_difference(
    list(get("scores_constrained_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred_free").jsonl("scores.jsonl")),
    list(get("scores_untuned_val_e3p_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl")),
)
tuned_free = paired_difference(
    list(get("scores_constrained_tuned_val_main_0_pred_free").jsonl("scores.jsonl")), val_main
)
# a grammar helps the untuned model and does almost nothing for the tuned one (@sec-constrained-decoding)
assert untuned_free["low"] > 0
assert abs(tuned_free["difference"]) < 0.005 and tuned_free["difference"] < untuned_free["difference"] / 4

RANKS = {4: "rank4", 8: "rank8", 16: "main", 32: "rank32", 64: "rank64"}
rank_scores = {r: list(get(f"scores_tuned_val_{n}_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl")) for r, n in RANKS.items()}
rank_acc = {r: bootstrap_accuracy(v)["accuracy"] for r, v in rank_scores.items()}
rank_vs_16 = {r: paired_difference(rank_scores[r], rank_scores[16]) for r in RANKS if r != 16}
spread = max(rank_acc.values()) - min(rank_acc.values())
# every rank from 4 to 64 is within a few points of the others, and none is told apart from rank 16 (@sec-rank-sweep)
assert spread < 0.03
assert not any(d["excludes_zero"] for d in rank_vs_16.values())


The book fine-tunes a small model, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, on one desktop GPU to answer the questions of ConvFinQA. A LoRA adapter of rank 16 teaches it to write each answer as a program in a small language, and the program is run to get the number. The adapter holds 33 million weights, 0.82% of the model’s, and took 3.9 hours to train.
On the development split, 1,490 turns that no choice of the book was made on, the fine-tuned model gets 81.3% of the answers right when its own earlier answers are the history of the conversation, and 90.3% when it is given the right ones (Chapter 16). The best prompt for the untuned model, with three worked examples, gets 56.8%, and the training prompt without examples 1.1%. The fine-tuned model is 24.5 points ahead of the first and 80.2 points ahead of the second, and the intervals of both differences (from resampling whole report pages) stay above zero. The comparison rests on one training seed.
The experiments on the validation split showed four more things:

Training took the validation loss from 2.21 to 0.036, with the lowest value at step 250 of 342 (Chapter 12).
After fine-tuning, writing the program in Python or in the small language makes no difference: the paired difference is -0.3 points, and its interval includes zero (Chapter 14).
A grammar that forces a valid program lifts the untuned model by +3.3 points, and the fine-tuned one by +0.1 (Chapter 15).
Ranks from 4 to 64 end within 2.1 points of each other, and none of the other ranks is told apart from rank 16 (Chapter 17).

Three commands reproduce the result without the book. train-adapter downloads the data and the base model if they are missing, trains the adapter with the settings of the main run on the training and validation splits (the development split is not read), and writes the adapter, with a file that records what it was trained from, to outputs/adapter:
uv run train-adapter
Training on a GPU is not bit-for-bit repeatable (Chapter 8), so a new adapter lands close to the book’s numbers and not on them. To ask the model about a page, print-example prints one conversation of the dataset as JSON (with --show-gold, also its questions and answers), and chat takes a page of that form, the three fields pre_text, table and post_text, and answers questions about it, one at a time, from the terminal:
uv run print-example dev:3 > page.json
uv run chat --page page.json
uv run chat --page page.json -q "what was the equipment rents payable in 2008?" -q "and in 2007?"
chat writes the program the model gave and the number it evaluates to, and keeps the model’s own programs as the history of the conversation, as in the predicted-history setting above.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Terms are in alphabetical order. Each chapter links a term here the first time it uses it, and each entry ends with the chapter where the term is developed.

AdamW

The optimizer of the book’s training runs: Adam, with weight decay applied to the weights directly and not through the gradient. The runs use no weight decay. See Chapter 8.

adapter

The small set of trained matrices that LoRA adds to a frozen model. It is saved on its own, and the base model is not changed. See Chapter 9.

alpha

The scale of a LoRA update: the correction is multiplied by \(\alpha / r\). The sweep sets \(\alpha = 2r\), so the multiplier is 2 at every rank. See Chapter 9.

artifact

A named result saved in artifacts/, made by a builder function that a chapter declares. It is rebuilt only when it, one of its inputs or the code it uses has changed. See Chapter 1.

attention

The layer in which each position takes a weighted mix of the values of the positions it can see, with weights from the match between its query and their keys. See Chapter 5.

base model

A model that has only been pretrained to predict the next token of a large body of text, and not post-trained to follow instructions. See Chapter 6.

bfloat16 and mixed precision

bfloat16 (bf16) is a 16-bit number format with the range of 32-bit floats and fewer digits of precision. Mixed-precision training does the arithmetic in bf16 over weights that are kept in 32-bit precision. See Chapter 8.

bounded grammar

A grammar that also limits each number to the digits that the gold programs use, where the plain grammar allows any number. See Section 15.8.

byte-level BPE

The way Qwen’s tokenizer splits text: byte-pair encoding over bytes. It starts from single bytes and merges the pairs that occur most often, so any text can be encoded. See Chapter 4.

causal mask

The mask that stops a position from attending to the ones after it. It lets one pass over a sequence train the prediction at every position, with each prediction seeing only what comes before it. See Chapter 5.

chat template

A small program shipped with the tokenizer that wraps each message of a conversation in the model’s own role markers and joins them into one string. See Chapter 6.

constrained decoding

Decoding in which a grammar removes, at each step, the tokens that cannot continue a valid output. It guarantees the form of the output, not that the output ends or is right. See Chapter 15.

cosine schedule

The learning rate of the training runs: a short linear warmup to the peak value, then a decay along a cosine curve towards zero. See Chapter 8.

decoder-only

A transformer made only of decoder blocks, in which every position attends to the earlier ones. Qwen3 is one. See Chapter 5.

development split (dev)

ConvFinQA’s own development split, used here as the test set. It is touched only for the final reported numbers, after the configuration is frozen. See Chapter 10.

DSL

The domain-specific language of ConvFinQA’s programs: a list of steps such as divide(#0, 181001), each with one of six operations, where #k is the result of an earlier step. See Chapter 3.

effective batch

The number of conversations whose gradients are combined for one optimizer step. When they do not fit in memory at once, gradient accumulation reaches it with several smaller micro-batches. See Chapter 8.

effective number of directions

For a LoRA update, \(1 / \sum p^2\), where \(p\) is the share of its squared norm held by each direction. It equals the rank if the directions share the norm evenly, and 1 if one direction holds all of it. See Section 17.6.1.

entropy

A measure of how spread out a probability distribution over the next token is: zero when one token has all the probability, and largest when every token is equally likely. See Chapter 4.

example set

A fixed group of complete training conversations written into a prompt as examples. See Chapter 11.

execution accuracy

The share of turns where the answer of the model’s program equals the gold answer after rounding to five decimal places. An output that is not a valid program, or does not execute, counts as wrong. See Chapter 3 and Chapter 13.

exposure bias

The mismatch left by teacher forcing: the model is trained on gold earlier turns, but when it is used it sees its own earlier outputs, which can be wrong. See Chapter 6.

few-shot and zero-shot

A prompt is few-shot when it contains worked examples, and zero-shot when it has none. See Chapter 7.

full fine-tuning

Training every weight of the model, where LoRA trains a small adapter. See Chapter 8.

gold history and predicted history

The two ways to fill the earlier turns of a prompt when a conversation is scored. With gold history they are the dataset’s own programs; with predicted history they are the model’s own outputs, mistakes included, so errors can compound. Predicted history is the headline setting. See Chapter 11.

gradient accumulation and clipping

Accumulation adds up the gradients of several micro-batches before one optimizer step. Clipping rescales a gradient whose norm is above a limit. See Chapter 8.

grammar

A formal description of the outputs that are allowed. Here it is a context-free grammar written in EBNF, for the DSL or for Python. See Chapter 15.

greedy decoding

Choosing the highest-scoring token at every step. It is deterministic, and every evaluation of the book uses it unless it says otherwise. See Chapter 4.

grouped-query attention

Attention in which several query heads share one key and value head, which makes the KV cache smaller. See Chapter 5.

instruct model

A base model that has been post-trained to follow instructions and to answer in a chat format. See Chapter 6.

invalid output

An output that is not a valid program or does not execute. It counts as wrong, and the evaluation reports its share next to the accuracy, by cause. See Chapter 13.

KV cache

The keys and values of every token already processed, kept so that generating the next token does not recompute them. See Chapter 5.

labels

The tokens that the loss is computed on. In this book they are the answer tokens and their end marker; every other token of a conversation is masked out. See Chapter 10.

learning rate

The size of the step that the optimizer takes along the gradient. See Chapter 8.

literal check

A check on the numbers a program is written with: whether they match those of the gold program, as text and as values, and whether each comes from the page. See Chapter 13.

logits

The scores that the model gives to every token of its vocabulary at a position, before they are turned into probabilities. See Chapter 4.

logits processor

A function that edits the logits after the model produces them and before a token is chosen. Constrained decoding is one. See Chapter 4.

LoRA

Low-rank adaptation: the weights of the model are frozen, and each adapted matrix gets an update that is the product of two thin matrices, so only those are trained. See Chapter 9.

loss

The number that training makes smaller: the negative log probability that the model gives to the gold tokens, averaged over the label tokens. See Chapter 8.

main run

The LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B on the DSL whose adapter the later chapters use. See Chapter 12.

merging an adapter

Adding the adapter’s update into the base weights, so the model runs without the adapter. It is the same function in 32-bit precision and not exactly in bf16. See Chapter 9.

negative log-likelihood

The loss of a sequence: the sum, or mean, of the surprisals of its tokens. See Chapter 7.

number-selection turn

A turn whose program is only a number copied from the page, with no operation. All other turns are lists of steps. See Chapter 3.

paired bootstrap

An interval for the difference between two systems scored on the same turns. It resamples whole report pages (with every conversation written from them), since the turns of one conversation, and the conversations of one page, are not independent, and computes both accuracies on each resample. An interval that excludes zero is a clear difference. See Section 11.4.2.

perplexity

The exponential of the mean surprisal: the model is as uncertain, on average, as if it were choosing among that many equally likely tokens. See Chapter 7.

post-training

The training that turns a pretrained model into an instruct model, such as supervised fine-tuning, distillation and reinforcement learning. See Chapter 6.

pretraining

The first stage of training, in which the model learns to predict the next token on a large body of text. See Chapter 6.

program accuracy

The share of turns where the model’s program is the gold program by the rule of the official ConvFinQA script: the programs are compared as expressions, so the operands of add and multiply may come in either order, and the arguments are compared as exact text. It is stricter than execution accuracy. See Chapter 13.

QLoRA

LoRA on a base model whose weights are stored in a low-precision, quantized format, to save memory. See Chapter 9.

rank

The number of directions between the two thin matrices of a LoRA update, and so the largest rank the update can have. See Chapter 9.

rank sweep

The same fine-tuning run at several values of the LoRA rank, compared on the same turns. See Chapter 17.

residual connection

The addition of a layer’s input to its output, so the layer learns a change to its input and not a replacement. See Chapter 5.

rotary position embedding

The way Qwen3 encodes position: queries and keys are rotated by an angle that depends on the position, so an attention score depends on the distance between two tokens. See Chapter 5.

sampling and temperature

Sampling draws the next token from the probabilities. The temperature divides the logits first: a low value sharpens the distribution towards greedy decoding, and a high one flattens it. See Chapter 4.

scale check

A check on whether an answer is the gold answer times, or divided by, a power of ten, which is a different mistake from a wrong number. See Chapter 13.

self-consistency

Sampling several programs at a temperature, dropping those that do not run, and taking the answer that most of them agree on. See Chapter 13.

singular values

The strengths of the independent directions of a matrix. For a LoRA update they show how its size is spread over its directions. See Chapter 12.

smoke run

A short run of the 0.5B model with the same recipe, to test the training code before the main run. See Chapter 12.

softmax

The function that turns logits into probabilities that are positive and sum to one. See Chapter 4.

supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

Training a model on example outputs with a next-token loss. See Chapter 6.

surprisal

The negative log of the probability the model gave to a token, in nats. See Chapter 7.

system message

The first message of a prompt, which tells the model what its task and its output format are. See Chapter 11.

teacher forcing

Training with the gold earlier tokens or turns in the input, whatever the model would have produced. See Chapter 6.

token and tokenizer

A token is a piece of text, usually a word or part of one, that the model reads and writes as one unit. The tokenizer turns text into token ids and back. See Chapter 4.

train-fit

The part of the training data that a run trains on: the training split without the validation conversations. See Chapter 12.

Type I and Type II conversations

Type I conversations break one FinQA question into a chain of turns. Type II conversations join two questions about the same page. See Chapter 2.

validation split

A tenth of the training conversations, grouped by page, held out for the choices of the book. The tuning is done on it, and the development split is kept for the final numbers. See Chapter 10.

warmup

The first steps of a run, in which the learning rate rises linearly from zero to its peak. See Chapter 8.

weight decay

A term that pulls each weight a little towards zero at every step. See Chapter 8.
